final.title: The three doors
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A famous puzzle with a real mechanism (what the host knows) that tallies and the three-cases board make clear without formulas; it is distinct from bayes-theorem's base-rate grid.
build 5: A seeded game simulation with stay/switch tallies, an enumeration of prize positions and an n-door generalisation is a tiny, fully honest model.
final.verifyNote: No catalogue page covers it. bayes-theorem counts test results on a grid of 1,000 people and never models a host's informed choice. The probabilities are correct (2/3 against 1/3), and the pitfall about a random host giving 1/2 is the standard result (Brilliant, Encyclopedia of Math). The model is a simple Monte Carlo with tallies and needs no data. Tallies and counts suit level 0, and the ten-door version is a sound way to build intuition.

final.title: Shapes that tile a floor
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Fitting corners around a point until they close one full turn is a clear, buildable mechanism that answers a real question and is distinct from chaos-fractals, though it builds on angles-as-turns.

build 5: Fitting regular polygons around a vertex by interior angle, flooding the plane for the three regular tilings, and an Escher tile whose edited edge is translated to the opposite edge are clean geometric constructions.
final.verifyNote: It is distinct, since no catalogue page covers tiling, and it is level 0 with an L0 prerequisite (angles-as-turns, in the pool). It is buildable as a geometric construction. But the takeaway as written is false for shapes in general. Every triangle and every quadrilateral tiles, and Rao (2017) completed the list of 15 families of convex pentagons that tile. The rule "corners fit into one full turn" only decides the case of regular polygons tiling alone. The takeaway and pitfall need to say "regular". The leadsTo link to states-of-matter is a weak tie but acceptable (crystal lattices).

fix.takeaway: A regular shape (all sides and corners equal) tiles a floor on its own only when copies of its corner fit together into exactly one full turn, which equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons do and regular pentagons and octagons do not.
fix.pitfall: Regular pentagons do not tile, but some irregular pentagons do (fifteen families of convex pentagons are known, and a 2017 proof says there are no more), and every triangle and every four-sided shape tiles. So the page must say 'this regular pentagon', never 'pentagons'.

final.title: Why triangles are stiff
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A square frame folding and a triangle holding firm is a pure mechanism a 10-year-old can build and test, and it is a well-scoped level-0 step before bridges-structures without its forces.

build 4: A pin-jointed stick frame solved by position-based distance constraints (Verlet) shows the square folding and the triangle holding, and a rigidity count can score the fewest-sticks challenge; the solver is level-1 code but the observable is level 0.
final.verifyNote: It is distinct from bridges-structures, which colours members by tension and compression under load. This page is about the rigidity of a pin-jointed frame (a mechanism against a structure), and the pitfall keeps the two apart. The claim is correct: the pin-jointed triangle is the only polygon that cannot deform, and triangulation makes a frame rigid. A small constraint solver (or springs) that shows the motions still allowed is easy to build in the browser and needs no data. It is honest at level 0 and grounded in the KS1/KS2 design and technology wording on stiffening structures.

final.title: Cellular automata
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A topic promoted from the catalogue's reserve, with editable rules and patterns that emerge from them, honest at level 1 and distinct from chaos-fractals' continuous systems.
build 5: Game of Life on a modest grid and elementary 1D rules from an 8-bit table are exact, cheap algorithms that run at interactive rates in SVG.
final.verifyNote: Against the existing catalogue it is distinct: chaos-fractals is continuous, and turing-machines is a tape machine. 'Cellular automata' is on the Reserve list, the level is honest for level 1, and the model is trivial to run in the browser. But the selection also contains life-on-a-grid (level 0), which already paints cells, steps Conway's Game of Life, finds blinkers and gliders and edits the rule numbers. Half of this page, and its pitfall about gliders, would repeat that page. The fix narrows this one to what the level-0 page lacks: one-dimensional elementary rules and their 8-bit lookup table, the space of 256 rules and Wolfram's four classes, rule 30's deterministic randomness, rule 90's Sierpinski triangle, rule 184 as a traffic model that conserves cars, and rule 110's universality. Life becomes a level-0 prerequisite (allowed, since it is not above level 1).

fix.interaction: Set the eight bits of a one-dimensional rule by clicking its lookup table, and run it from a single live cell or a random row, each generation drawn as a new line below the last. Rule 90 draws a Sierpinski triangle, rule 30 looks random, rule 110 carries colliding structures, and rule 184 moves cars along a road that jams once more than half the cells are full. Step through all 256 rules and sort them into Wolfram's four classes (die out, repeat, look random, build structures), with a count of live cells over time to compare rules.
fix.takeaway: A rule that only looks at a cell and its two neighbours, applied everywhere at once, can die out, repeat, look random or build moving structures, and changing one bit of the rule can switch between them.
fix.pitfall: Rule 30 looks random but is completely determined: the same starting row always gives the same pattern. And most rules do not make complexity; they die out or repeat, and only a few, like rule 110, build lasting structures.
fix.overlapWith: life-on-a-grid (proposed, level 0): that page plays Conway's two-dimensional Game of Life; this page opens the rule itself as an 8-bit table in one dimension, surveys all 256 rules and their classes, and shows a CA as a traffic model and as a universal computer. chaos-fractals shows complexity in continuous systems; turing-machines uses a tape and head, not a grid of cells updating at once.
fix.why: Wikipedia, Elementary cellular automaton and Rule 184 (traffic model): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_184 ; 'Cellular automata' is listed in the catalogue's Reserve.

final.title: Exponentials & logarithms
judgeNotes: build 5: Repeated multiplication, a linear/log axis toggle and a slide rule made of log-length bars are closed-form geometry with no data, a small, honest level-1 model.

fit-level 4: A core gap: radioactivity and epidemics use exponentials but no page isolates multiply-versus-add growth or explains the log as a count of steps. The slide rule and log axis give the graphic a real mechanism to show.
final.verifyNote: The catalogue's Reserve names this topic. radioactivity (half-life decay), epidemics (case doubling) and rockets (the rocket equation) each use an exponential inside a mechanism, but none isolates growth by a constant factor, the log axis or the logarithm as a count of steps. The overlapping pool entry growing-patterns (level 0) was not selected. Level 1 is honest: Common Core HSF-LE puts exponential models and logarithms as solutions of a*b^(ct)=d in high school. It runs as pure arithmetic, curves and a slide-rule construction. The takeaway is sound, reading a logarithm as the count of factor steps, fractional counts included. The pitfall is a real misconception, correctly stated. Small improvement: the entry says the log-scale slope 'is the growth rate'; strictly it is the logarithm of the growth factor per step, so the narrative should phrase it as 'a fixed growth factor'.

final.title: Game theory: why cooperate?
judgeNotes: build 5: An Axelrod-style round-robin of five fixed strategies, a copy-the-winner population update and a spatial grid game are cheap agent simulations that run easily in the browser, and the honest model needs no equations at level 1.

fit-level 4: An Axelrod tournament is a vivid, popular mechanism with no existing equivalent and is honest at level 1. Its spatial-grid finale duplicates the one in evolutionary-game-theory, so the grid belongs on only one of the two pages.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from the catalogue: evolution has no choosing agents or payoffs, and reinforcement-learning is a single agent. 'Game theory' is on the Reserve list, and the level-3 replicator-dynamics entries (evolutionary-games, evolutionary-game-theory) were not selected. Level 1 is honest. The model is an exact algorithm: an iterated prisoner's dilemma round-robin, imitation dynamics, and a Nowak-May spatial grid. The pitfall is factually right: Axelrod himself notes tit for tat never did better than the player it faced and won on total score. The 2014 reanalysis (PMC4520619) confirms its success depends on payoffs, tournament design and noise. The takeaway, though, states a universal law ('beats pure selfishness') that the entry's own pitfall contradicts: under noise, or among enough defectors, tit for tat loses. The fix softens the takeaway to 'can outscore', with the conditions observable in the toy.

fix.takeaway: When the same players meet again and again, strategies that start nice, hit back and forgive can outscore pure selfishness, so cooperation can take hold among players who each look after only themselves, unless the games are too short or too few others cooperate.

final.title: Differential equations
judgeNotes: build 5: Slope fields and Euler or exact solution curves for the four named equations are a few arithmetic operations per arrow, a small honest model with no data.

fit-level 4: Slope fields with Euler stepping are the natural sequel to calculus and a true level-2 page, one of the few justified at that level. Keep the step-size blow-up brief so it doesn't duplicate numerical-stability.
final.verifyNote: This is a Reserve topic, and level 2 is honest (AP Calculus BC Unit 7 covers slope fields and Euler's method). Three problems remain. (a) Stepping by hand with Euler's method, shrinking the step and watching it converge or blow up is the whole of the proposed how-simulations-work (L1), and numerical-stability (L3) covers the blow-up, so the page would repeat both. (b) The spring and rabbits-and-foxes are second-order or two-variable systems: they cannot be drawn as a slope field in the (t, y) plane, and as phase-plane flows they belong to phase-portraits. (c) The pitfall overstates its case: a formula, when one exists, is a solution; the point is that most equations have none. Fix: keep the page to first-order equations dy/dt = f(t, y) and to slope fields and solution curves, with Euler only as 'follow the arrows'.

fix.interaction: Choose a rule for the slope at every point (growth in proportion to the amount, cooling toward room temperature, logistic growth with a ceiling, a fish stock under steady harvesting) and the plane of time against amount fills with small slope arrows; click anywhere to drop a starting value and watch a solution curve thread through the arrows. Drop several starts and see that curves never cross, that some settle on a level line and others run away from it, and raise the harvest until the level line vanishes and every curve crashes; where an exact formula exists, overlay it on the traced curve.
fix.takeaway: A differential equation says how fast something changes given where it is, and that rule plus a starting point fixes one curve through the field of arrows, which can be followed even when no formula exists.
fix.pitfall: Not every differential equation can be solved with a formula: most cannot, and the slope field still fixes each solution. Solution curves of one equation never cross, so two different futures cannot start from the same state.
fix.overlapWith: calculus finds the slope and area of a given curve; this page starts from the slope rule and finds the curve. how-simulations-work (L1) owns the step-size and accuracy story of Euler stepping, and phase-portraits (L3) owns two-variable systems such as springs and predator–prey; this page is the one-variable slope field, equilibria and their stability.

final.title: The brachistochrone & calculus of variations
judgeNotes: build 5: The bead's descent time is a 1D quadrature along a spline, and gradient descent on a dozen control points converging to the analytic cycloid (plus the catenary) runs at interactive rates; this is the real functional being minimised.

fit-level 4: The brachistochrone race is a classic, visual, wanted subject, and relaxing a curve toward the cycloid shows the real functional being minimized. That is honest level-3 content and distinct from newtons-laws.
final.verifyNote: Distinct: newtons-laws runs a cart along an editable track, but nothing in the catalogue optimises over whole curves. Level 3 is honest, because the brachistochrone and the catenary are standard material in university classical mechanics and calculus-of-variations courses. The model is real and cheap: the descent time is integrated along a discretised curve (the 1/sqrt(y) singularity at the start can be integrated), and gradient descent on a few dozen nodes runs at interactive rates. The catenary needs a length constraint (a Lagrange multiplier), which is also tractable. The pitfall is correct: the path dips below the end point when the horizontal distance exceeds π/2 times the drop. Two small fixes. The Euler–Lagrange equation is necessary, not sufficient, so the takeaway should say the optimum makes it hold rather than that a curve holding it beats every neighbour. And a brachistochrone is not an everyday object.

fix.takeaway: The fastest slide between two points is a curve, the cycloid, not the straight line, and at the optimum the Euler–Lagrange residual is zero all along the curve, so no small change to its shape makes the slide faster.
fix.pitfall: The best curve can dip below the end point and still win (it does whenever the horizontal distance is more than about π/2 times the drop), and the straight line is not 'almost as good': show it losing to the cycloid by a measured margin. A curve that satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation is stationary, not automatically the minimum.
fix.why: Fowler, Graduate Classical Mechanics, ch. 2 'The Calculus of Variations' (brachistochrone): https://phys.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Classical_Mechanics/Graduate_Classical_Mechanics_(Fowler)/02%3A_The_Calculus_of_Variations/2.05%3A_Fastest_Curve_for_Given_Horizontal_Distance ; demand: myPhysicsLab brachistochrone simulation https://www.myphysicslab.com/roller/brachistochrone-en.html

final.title: Phase portraits & stability
judgeNotes: build 5: Eigenvalues of a 2×2 matrix, a trace–determinant chart, a streamline field and RK4 trajectories for the pendulum, predator–prey and van der Pol systems through a Hopf bifurcation all run live, with no data.

fit-level 4: Classifying flows by eigenvalues on the trace-determinant chart, with linearizations laid over real flows and a Hopf bifurcation, is the standard university model. It is distinct from chaos-fractals and ecosystems.
final.verifyNote: Distinct enough and honestly at level 3: it is MIT 18.03 Unit IV. hamiltonian-phase-space (pool, L3) is about preserved area and Poincaré sections, not about classifying fixed points. The model is cheap to run in the browser. But the takeaway is factually wrong and contradicts the entry's own pitfall. 'Near each fixed point the real flow is the linear flow' holds only at hyperbolic points (Hartman–Grobman); at centers, and at the Hopf bifurcation the page itself shows, it fails (MIT 18.03SC's structural-stability note gives a linearised center that settles nothing). 'Long-run behavior read off from a few fixed points' also ignores the limit cycles the page creates. Fix the takeaway, and add the proposed L2 differential-equations as a prerequisite.

fix.takeaway: Near a fixed point whose eigenvalues have nonzero real parts, the real flow looks like its linearization, so a few fixed points and their eigenvalues sketch the whole portrait; when the eigenvalues reach the imaginary axis, as at a Hopf bifurcation, the nonlinear terms take over and a limit cycle can appear that no fixed point predicts.
fix.overlapWith: chaos-fractals shows sensitivity to initial conditions and the logistic map's cascade, and the pool's hamiltonian-phase-space is about area preservation and Poincaré sections; this page classifies flows in the plane by their fixed points and eigenvalues and shows where linearization stops working (ecosystems shows one predator–prey cycle at level 1 as curves, not as a portrait).
fix.why: MIT OCW 18.03SC, Unit IV, Linearization near critical points (including its structural-stability note on borderline centers): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-03sc-differential-equations-fall-2011/pages/unit-iv-first-order-systems/linearization-near-critical-points

final.title: Random graphs & the giant component
judgeNotes: build 5: Erdős–Rényi graphs on a few hundred nodes with union-find for the giant component, preferential attachment and grid bond percolation are cheap seeded simulations, and the threshold appears in the live plot.

fit-level 4: The giant component's sudden appearance at average degree 1 is a striking emergent mechanism, and preferential attachment adds real network science. No existing page covers network structure itself.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from every existing page (internet routes packets over a fixed network, epidemics has an R0 threshold in time not a structural one, pagerank ranks a hand-built web); Erdos-Renyi with a few hundred nodes and union-find runs at interactive rates; level 3 is honest (network science / random graph theory course, MIT 6.207). Two weaknesses: the page tries three toys (ER, preferential attachment, grid percolation), and preferential attachment's takeaway (hubs) is a different idea not observable in the same graphic; and the takeaway says 'suddenly' while the pitfall rightly says a finite graph is rounded. Narrow to ER with a node-count control so the knee sharpening is the thing seen, keep grid percolation as the second view of the same threshold, and qualify the takeaway.

fix.interaction: Slide the average degree of a random graph and watch components merge, coloured by size: the largest component's share of the nodes stays near zero until the average degree passes 1, then climbs, plotted live against degree. Raise the number of nodes from 50 to a few thousand and rerun the sweep: the curve's knee at degree 1 sharpens toward a corner. A second view opens bonds on a square grid at random and shows a spanning cluster appearing at its own threshold, near half the bonds open.
fix.takeaway: In a large random network, adding links does not connect it gradually: a giant connected piece appears abruptly once each node has about one link on average, and the bigger the network, the sharper that switch.

final.title: The bootstrap & permutation tests
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Permutation tests, the bootstrap and power are real university statistics with a mechanism the graphic shows directly (rebuilding the null distribution), and the page is clearly distinct from central-limit-theorem and learning-from-data.

build 5: Permutation tests, bootstrap and power curves are a few thousand cheap resamples of 344 rows, an honest algorithm at interactive rates; palmerpenguins is confirmed CC0 (the authors ask, as a courtesy and not a licence term, to be contacted before publication).
final.verifyNote: Data is fine (palmerpenguins is CC0, confirmed). But two problems. Duplication: the power plot, the false-positive rate and the 'run twenty null comparisons and one is significant' demo are exactly the core of the proposed level-3 clinical-trials page (power, false positives, multiple outcomes, early stopping). Level: p-values, power and Type I error, and even simulation-based permutation tests, are AP Statistics / first-year intro-stats material (Hesterberg's cited paper is about the undergraduate intro curriculum), i.e. level 2, not level 3. A small change fixes both: narrow to resampling itself and make it genuinely university-level by checking the bootstrap against a known population, where its interval coverage can be measured and seen to fall short at small n or for statistics like the maximum (Efron & Tibshirani; Hesterberg 2015 notes percentile intervals undercover for small n).

fix.title: The bootstrap & permutation tests
fix.interaction: Compare flipper length between two species of real penguins: shuffle the group labels thousands of times to build the histogram of differences that chance alone produces, and read the p-value as where the observed difference falls in it. Resample each group with replacement to build a bootstrap distribution and a confidence interval for the difference and for a regression slope. Then switch to a known simulated population, repeat the whole procedure hundreds of times, and count how often the interval catches the true value: drag the sample size down, skew the population or ask for the maximum instead of the mean, and watch the coverage fall below 95%.
fix.takeaway: Resampling rebuilds the chance distribution from the data itself, and it works only as well as the sample stands in for the population: with small or skewed samples the intervals miss the truth more often than they claim.
fix.pitfall: A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and a bootstrap interval is not guaranteed to have its stated coverage: the bootstrap does not cure a small sample. The coverage counter must show the shortfall, not a reassuring 95%.
fix.overlapWith: learning-from-data: that page fits a curve and shows overfitting with a held-out set; this page asks whether a difference or slope is real by rebuilding the chance distribution from the data. clinical-trials (proposed) owns power, false positives and multiple comparisons; this page leaves those to it and is about resampling and its coverage.

final.title: Taylor series & where they stop working
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Showing the radius of convergence set by a complex singularity is a real and surprising mechanism; plain Taylor polynomials would be level 2, but the complex-disk explanation makes level 3 honest, and it is distinct from calculus.
build 5: Partial sums, the disk of convergence reaching the singularities at ±i, and Chebyshev interpolation are exact cheap computations, and blow-up beyond |x| = 1 is visible at a glance.
final.verifyNote: Not a duplicate: calculus shows only tangent and area; fourier-transform sums sines, not powers. Level is borderline: Taylor polynomials and radius/interval of convergence are AP Calculus BC (high school) material, which alone would be level 2; what makes it level 3 is explaining the radius by the nearest complex singularity (complex analysis), so that disk must be the core, not a side panel. One factual slip: the series for 1/(1+x^2) does not 'fit perfectly up to |x| = 1'; it converges only for |x| < 1, slowly near 1, and diverges at |x| = 1 itself. Takeaway should say the function is analytic at the centre. All buildable as closed-form polynomials; prerequisites calculus and complex-numbers are level 2, fine.

fix.interaction: Pick a function and add Taylor terms one at a time with a slider: the polynomial hugs e^x and sin x ever further from the center, but for 1/(1 + x²) it closes in only for |x| < 1 and swings ever wilder beyond, however many terms are added. A linked complex plane shows the disk of convergence and the function's singularities at ±i: the disk stops exactly where it touches the nearest one; drag the center along the real line and the disk, and the stretch of the real line the polynomials fit, resize to match. A last toggle overlays Chebyshev interpolation, which fits the whole interval anyway.
fix.takeaway: The Taylor series of a function converges exactly out to its nearest singularity in the complex plane, even when nothing goes wrong on the real line.
fix.pitfall: More terms do not always mean a better fit: outside the radius each new term makes the polynomial worse, and a function can be smooth everywhere on the real line and still have a finite radius. Do not claim convergence on the boundary circle: for 1/(1 + x²) the series diverges at x = ±1.

final.title: Why the sky is blue & sunsets red
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A classic question children ask, answered by a real scattering model scrubbed through a day, with no formulas needed; nothing on the site covers scattering.

build 4: Single-scattering Rayleigh along the air path, converted with the CMFs the site already ships, is the honest model and cheap. The ASTM G173 AM0 column's licence is unconfirmed (ASTM is copyrighted, NREL redistributes it); a 5772 K blackbody or NASA's public-domain TSIS/SORCE solar spectrum would remove that risk.
final.verifyNote: Distinct: light-optics refracts and disperses light and never scatters it, and no catalogue page explains the colour of the sky. Level 0 is honest, since the fourth-power law stays hidden in the model and the reader only scrubs the Sun and thickens the air. The model (single Rayleigh scattering along an air path, plus a lightly coloured haze term) runs easily in the browser. The takeaway and pitfall are correct (violet: less of it in sunlight and lower eye sensitivity). The data question is the weak point, and the entry admits it. The licence of the ASTM G173 AM0 column is unconfirmed: the ASTM standard is copyrighted, and I found no statement on NREL's file. The CVRL/CIE colour-matching functions also carry no stated licence (CIE's own data pages show none). Under the 'default refute on data' rule, switch both to sources with no data question. Above the atmosphere, a 5772 K Planck spectrum gives the same screen colour as AM0 (Fraunhofer lines don't change a colour). The CIE 1931 functions can come from the published analytic fit of Wyman, Sloan and Shirley (2013), which is a formula. Optionally keep AM0 as a cited comparison once its licence is settled.

fix.needs: None that needs a licence: sunlight above the air as a Planck spectrum at the Sun's effective temperature (5772 K, the IAU nominal value), and the CIE 1931 colour-matching functions from the analytic fit of Wyman, Sloan & Shirley (JCGT 2013), a formula. Optional, once its licence is confirmed: the ASTM G173-03 AM0 'Etr' column from NLR/NREL as a cited cross-check.
fix.needsSource: Two spectra from one model: the Sun's disc is the Planck spectrum attenuated by Rayleigh scattering (fourth power of wavelength) along the air path for the Sun's height; the sky patch is the light scattered into the line of sight along that path and attenuated on its way to the eye (single scattering), with optional haze of weak colour dependence; both are turned into screen colour with the analytic CIE 1931 fit. No data files: the Planck law and the fit are formulas. The ASTM G173 file (licence unconfirmed; the standard itself is ASTM copyright) and the CVRL tables (no licence stated) are avoided.

final.title: Floating, sinking & boats
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Floating explained by the weight of the water pushed aside, with the clay ball and clay bowl, is a must-have formula-free mechanism that no existing page covers.
build 5: Solving for the waterline where the displaced area's weight equals the object's weight on a 2D hull polygon is an honest, fast model, and a few handbook densities are uncopyrightable facts.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from the catalogue: states-of-matter only shows ice less dense than water inside a molecular box, and flight is about lift, not buoyancy. Level 0 is honest (KS3 upthrust, PhET Buoyancy Basics), and the model (Archimedes with a waterline from a hull's cross-section) is easily buildable. Handbook densities are facts. Note for the curator: the pool also has sink-or-float (chemistry) and fluid-pressure-buoyancy (physics), so these are probably to be merged or chosen between. Two factual faults. (1) The takeaway says a thing floats when it pushes aside MORE than its own weight. A floating object pushes aside exactly its own weight. The rule is that it floats if it can push aside its own weight before it is completely under, and as written the takeaway invites the opposite misconception. (2) A 'scale under the tank' does not show the pushed-aside water: for a stone resting on the bottom, it rises by the stone's whole weight. The honest instrument is an overflow (eureka) can spilling into a cup on a scale, set beside a spring balance holding the object.

fix.takeaway: A thing floats if it can push aside its own weight of water (or air) before it is completely under, which is why the same lump of clay sinks as a ball and floats as a bowl.
fix.interaction: Lower objects into a brim-full tank (a stone, an apple, a wooden block, a steel ball, a ball of modelling clay): the water each one pushes aside spills into a cup on a scale, and a spring balance holding the object shows it getting lighter as it goes in. Each one sinks, or settles where the spilled water weighs as much as it does. Reshape the clay from a ball into a bowl and the same lump floats; load it with marbles until it goes under. Change the water to salt water or to oil and see who floats now; finally warm the air inside a balloon and watch it rise through the surrounding air the same way.

final.title: Magnets & poles
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A core primary-school subject with a real mechanism (poles, falling-off pull, induced magnetism in a clip); it is fully level 0 and distinct from the level-2 electromagnetism page, and it is a natural lead-in to it.

build 4: A Gilbert two-pole model with inverse-square forces, a field sampled for the compass and filings, and an induced pole pair for steel clips are all cheap to compute, and an honest level-0 approximation as long as the page notes that poles are a model.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from electromagnetism (level 2: charges, field lines, induction), and squarely NGSS 3-PS2-3 / KS2 Year 3. Level 0 is honest. The Gilbert two-pole model with inverse-square pole forces, a field-direction field for the filings and compass, and an induced dipole in steel is a real, cheap model; it needs no data. Note for the curator: the pool also has magnets-and-electromagnets (physics) and compass-and-magnetic-poles (earth), which overlap at this level. The fault is the pitfall: 'only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt' repeats a misconception. Common austenitic stainless steels (304/316, cutlery and sinks) are not attracted or only barely, while many alloys and some rare-earth metals are. The takeaway and the cut-magnet point are correct.

fix.pitfall: A magnet does not attract all metals, nor even all steel: it pulls iron, nickel, cobalt and most steels, but not aluminium, copper, gold or many stainless-steel spoons and sinks. And cutting a magnet never separates its poles: each piece has two.

final.title: Shadows & pinholes
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Straight-line light explaining shadow size, soft edges and the pinhole image is core KS2 content, shown purely by geometry, and it never overlaps the refraction bench.
build 5: 2D ray projection from point and extended sources past polygons gives the umbra, penumbra and pinhole inversion exactly, and it is cheap and fully honest.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from light-optics, which only bends rays through lenses and prisms; blocking rays, umbra and penumbra, and the pinhole image are not on any page, and the eclipse case stays with sun-earth-moon. The level is honest: KS2 Year 3 and Year 6 'Light' cover this, it needs no formulas, and shadow size is a comparison. Ray projection past polygons from a point source or an extended one is a cheap geometric model and needs no data. The takeaway and the pitfall (shadow as an absence of light; phases are not Earth's shadow) are both correct.

final.title: Vibrations & sound
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A core KS2/KS3 and NGSS subject with a clear mechanism (vibration passed along through air: pitch, loudness, the bell jar) that is a true beginner on-ramp to waves-interference and does not duplicate its interference and harmonics.

build 4: Cantilever frequency scaling as 1/L squared, a 1D mass-spring chain for the air, distance falloff and Web Audio tones are all small and honest. The bell jar works by reducing the chain's coupling and density.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from waves-interference, which has two sources, harmonics and Doppler but never shows what sound is: one vibrating source, a longitudinal push passed along a chain, the need for a medium. The level fits KS2 Year 4, and a ruler that sounds higher when shortened (f ~ 1/L^2) plus a mass-spring chain is a real model. One small flaw: the takeaway says 'with no air nothing reaches the ear', which teaches that sound needs air specifically. Sound also travels through solids and water (the bell jar's stand leaks some), so the claim should be that it needs some material to pass the push along. Fixed by rewording the takeaway and adding this to the pitfall.

fix.takeaway: A sound is a wobble passed along through the air: a faster wobble is a higher note, a bigger wobble a louder one, and with nothing in between to pass it on, nothing reaches the ear.
fix.pitfall: Sound does not travel as air flying from the source to the ear; each bit of air jiggles in place and passes the push on. Louder is not higher: loudness and pitch are two different things. Sound needs some material to carry it, not air in particular: it travels through water, wood and metal too, and only empty space stops it.

final.title: Why music has twelve notes
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: An appealing, distinctive question with a real mechanism (frequency ratios, beats and a roughness model, dividing the octave equally) that waves-interference does not cover, at an honest level 1.

build 5: Equal-division arithmetic, the Plomp-Levelt/Sethares roughness formula, waveform overlays and Web Audio synthesis form a real, tiny model whose results (the 12-EDO fifth within 2 cents) are visible and audible.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from waves-interference, which covers beats and string harmonics but not which intervals fit together or how the octave is divided. Level 1 is fair (frequency ratios and logarithmic steps), synthesized tones plus the published Plomp-Levelt roughness curve make an honest model, and no data is needed. The takeaway overclaims in two ways. First, 5- and 7-step divisions also land within about 20 cents of the fifth, so twelve is not simply 'the smallest ladder that lands close'. What makes 12 special is that 7/12 is a continued-fraction convergent of log2(3/2), putting its fifth within 2 cents (the next good ones are 41 and 53). Second, the twelve-key keyboard came from chains of fifths in Pythagorean and meantone tunings, centuries before equal temperament, so equal temperament is not why pianos have twelve keys. Fixed by narrowing the takeaway and the interaction to what the graphic shows.

fix.interaction: A keyboard whose keys play, each note drawn as its wave; press two keys and the page plays them together and draws how the waves line up: an octave (double the frequency) repeats every cycle, a fifth (3:2) every two, while clashing pairs beat and a roughness meter (the Plomp-Levelt curve) rises. Slide a divider to cut the octave into 5, 7, 12, 19, 31 or 53 equal steps and read off how many cents each ladder misses the pure fifth and major third by; twelve is the first small ladder whose fifth lands within 2 cents. Compare an equal-tempered chord with a pure one by ear.
fix.takeaway: Notes sound smooth together when their frequencies are in simple ratios, and twelve equal steps per octave is the smallest small ladder whose fifth lands almost exactly on the pure 3:2.

final.title: The Ising model & phase transitions
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The canonical stat-mech model of a phase transition, with a clear Metropolis mechanism and the 1D no-transition case; it is distinct from states-of-matter.

build 5: A Metropolis 2D lattice of a few hundred spins on a side runs easily at interactive rates, and every claimed observation (domains, susceptibility peak, hysteresis, no 1D transition) comes straight out of it.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from states-of-matter, a level-1 molecular-dynamics box with no critical point or divergences. Level 3 is honest (statistical physics courses cover it, e.g. MIT OCW RES.8-010), its prerequisites are entropy (level 2) and the proposed level-3 partition-function, and Metropolis on a 2D lattice runs easily in the browser. Two physics errors. (a) The interaction says the magnetization 'jumps from zero to nearly full' at Tc, but the 2D Ising transition is continuous (second order): it rises steeply and continuously (beta = 1/8) as T falls below Tc. A jump would teach the first-order picture. (b) The takeaway says nearest-neighbour alignment 'alone' gives a sharp transition, yet the page itself shows that the one-dimensional chain has none, so dimension (at least two) must be in the takeaway. Also: near Tc, single-flip Metropolis slows down sharply (critical slowing down), so offer a Wolff cluster update, and the hysteresis loop only appears below Tc.

fix.interaction: Run a square lattice of spins with the Metropolis algorithm (or the Wolff cluster update, which stays fast near the critical point) and slide the temperature through Tc: domains grow out of noise, the magnetization rises steeply but continuously from zero as the lattice cools below Tc, and the susceptibility and heat capacity spike. Below Tc, apply a field and sweep it back and forth to trace a hysteresis loop; grow the lattice to see the peaks sharpen, and shrink it to a one-dimensional chain to see the transition vanish.
fix.takeaway: In two dimensions, nearest-neighbour alignment alone produces a phase transition at a definite temperature, sharp only in the limit of a large system, while a one-dimensional chain never orders.

final.title: Lasers
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: High visitor demand and a real rate-equation model (threshold, clamping, two-level saturation, Q-switching) that no existing page covers.
build 5: Four-level rate equations with a photon number are a small, stiff-but-easy ODE that shows threshold, clamping, relaxation oscillations and Q-switching honestly.
final.verifyNote: Not in the catalogue; it is the 'Lasers & LEDs' item in the Reserve list, and nearest pages (solar-cells, semiconductors) do not show stimulated emission, cavity threshold or inversion. Level 3 is honest (rate equations, Q-switching and relaxation oscillations are university laser-physics material, e.g. MIT 6.977), and its prerequisites (quantum-mechanics, level 3; oscillations-resonance, level 1) are within level. A few coupled rate-equation ODEs integrate easily at interactive rates, and no data is needed. The pitfall is correct (steady incoherent pumping of a two-level system saturates at N1 = N2). The takeaway's 'every extra pumped atom adds a photon' is the ideal case: non-radiative decay and pump-to-upper-level efficiency lower it, and only the mirror-transmitted fraction leaves. Softened accordingly.

fix.takeaway: A laser is a cavity in which stimulated emission out-competes loss, and above that threshold the inversion stops growing and nearly every extra pumped atom adds a photon to the same mode.

final.title: Dissolving: where does the sugar go?
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A core KS2/KS3 idea (dissolving is not melting or vanishing, there is a limit, drying brings it back) with a clear particle mechanism no existing page shows; prerequisite for several other level-0 candidates.
build 4: The same honest particle model as dissolving-sugar, plus evaporation that recrystallises the solute, with a dozen handbook solubility values. Keep this one and fold dissolving-sugar into it.
final.verifyNote: It is distinct from the catalogue (states-of-matter changes one substance's phase), but it nearly duplicates the pool candidate dissolving-sugar: a particle counter, warming, a saturation limit, nothing lost. Its dry-it-back step overlaps separating-mixtures (the evaporating dish) and growing-crystals. The takeaway is also wrong for half the page. Salt's solubility barely changes with temperature (about 35.7 to 39 g per 100 g of water from 0 to 100 °C), while sucrose's rises from about 179 to 487 g. So 'warm water takes more' holds for sugar only. 'Until no more will fit' teaches the misconception that saturation means running out of room between water particles. The fix narrows the page to what neither sibling shows: sugar and salt side by side, and how differently temperature affects them. It should be merged with dissolving-sugar, or that one dropped.

fix.interaction: Two glasses of water drawn as particles, one for sugar and one for salt, and a spoonful counter under each. One control at a time: tip in another spoonful, then slide the thermometer to warm both glasses. Each grain breaks into particles that wander off among the water particles until the water will take no more, and the rest sits on the bottom. Warming lets the sugar glass take spoonful after spoonful more, while the salt glass hardly takes any extra. At the end, let the water dry away and watch the same particles gather back into grains.
fix.takeaway: Dissolved sugar and salt have not vanished: their particles are spread among the water's, each glass of water takes only so much, and warming lets it take far more sugar but hardly any more salt.
fix.pitfall: Dissolving is not melting, and the sugar does not disappear or turn into water: every particle is still there, which is why the water tastes sweet and weighs more. A full glass is not 'out of room' between water particles: it stops because dissolving and grains re-forming have come into balance.
fix.overlapWith: dissolving-sugar (pool) and states-of-matter: states-of-matter changes the phase of one substance. This page compares two solids and shows that temperature raises how much sugar water will take but barely changes salt. It should be merged with dissolving-sugar rather than built alongside it.
fix.needs: Solubility of sucrose and of sodium chloride in water from 0 to 100 °C (about a dozen values) from the IUPAC-NIST Solubility Data Series, freely readable at NIST, or the ACS Middle School Chemistry tables; published facts, no dataset licence to clear.
fix.needsSource: About a dozen tabulated solubility values (IUPAC-NIST Solubility Data Series via NIST; ACS Middle School Chemistry, chapter 5 lesson 6); facts, no licence needed.

final.title: Salt on ice: roads and ice cream
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Salt blocking re-freezing and the ice-cream bath getting colder than ice is a surprising, distinct mechanism, though the heat-drawing half is hard to make honest for a 10-year-old without energy ideas.

build 4: Equilibrium on the NaCl brine liquidus (FHWA table, US government public domain) plus an energy balance for heat of fusion is an honest small model. The bath dropping below 0 °C and freezing the cream emerges from it.
final.verifyNote: No catalogue page covers freezing-point depression or freezing mixtures: states-of-matter covers only pure substances. Its level-0 framing works without formulas, using temperatures only as comparisons. The data source is real and public domain: FHWA-RD-95-202, Appendix B (freezing points of chemical solutions), is a US government work. The physics is right. NaCl brine's lowest freezing point is about −21 °C, the bath cools because melting absorbs heat, and the pitfall is correct. The one gap is that the interaction does not name its model. The honest model is the brine freezing-point curve plus a heat balance between ice, brine and cream, with the particle picture as illustration. A small edit makes that explicit and replaces the vague 'turn the cold down'.

fix.interaction: A block of ice drawn as a neat stack of water particles, with a thermometer. One control at a time: sprinkle salt, and salt particles get between the water particles at the surface so the stack cannot re-form, and the ice melts although the thermometer reads below freezing. Set the weather colder and the salt stops working; pour on more salt and see the point where extra salt no longer helps. Then put a bag of cream into the salted ice: the melting pulls heat out of the cream, the bath's thermometer drops below what plain ice could reach, and the cream freezes. Behind the picture runs the measured freezing-point curve of salt water and a running count of the heat that melting takes from the bath and the cream.

final.title: Why metal feels cold
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: It fixes a misconception everyone has with one finger, one control and a real conduction model, and no existing page covers it (it arguably belongs in physics rather than chemistry).

build 5: Two semi-infinite bodies in contact under 1D heat conduction, with real conductivity, density and heat capacity (thermal effusivity), give the contact temperature exactly at interactive rates from under ten public constants, and the result shows in the graphic.
final.verifyNote: It is distinct from entropy, levelled honestly for KS2 (Year 5 lists thermal conductivity among material properties), and buildable as 1D heat conduction between skin and object. The physics, though, is stated wrongly in two places. First, what sets the felt temperature is the contact temperature, which depends on each material's thermal effusivity sqrt(k·ρ·c) (conductivity, density and heat capacity together), not on conductivity alone. Physics-teaching papers flag 'conducts heat away faster' as the misleading version, so the model must use effusivity, even though the page never says the word. Second, metal feels hottest only when the room is warmer than the skin (above about 33 °C), not merely 'hot'.

fix.interaction: A table with a metal spoon, a wooden spoon, a plastic cup and a woollen glove, all at room temperature, with a thermometer that reads the same on each. Drag a finger onto any one: a strip of heat colour flows out of the fingertip into the object, fast into the metal and barely at all into the wool, and a 'feels like' dial follows the temperature where skin meets object. One control: the room temperature. Warm the room past the temperature of your hand and the order flips, so the same metal now feels hottest. The flow is a heat-conduction model in which each material uses its real conductivity, density and heat capacity.
fix.takeaway: Everything on the table is the same temperature; the metal feels cold because it draws heat out of your finger fastest, and when the room is warmer than your hand the same metal feels hottest.
fix.needs: Thermal conductivity, density and specific heat of skin, a metal (steel or aluminium), wood, plastic and wool: under twenty published constants from textbook tables or Wikipedia's material-property tables (CC BY-SA). The model combines them, because contact temperature depends on all three.
fix.pitfall: Metal is not colder than wood, and cold does not flow into your hand: heat flows out of it, and a thermometer shows the two objects equal. The page also should not say conductivity alone decides it: how much heat the material soaks up per degree matters too.

final.title: Chromatography: separating by stickiness
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Random partitioning that separates bands, plus the van Deemter optimum, is a real stochastic model a chemistry student learns, and no existing page covers it.

build 5: A random walk of molecules hopping between mobile and stationary phases by partition coefficient, with path-length and diffusion noise, separates and broadens bands and produces the van Deemter minimum from a sweep, with no data needed.
final.verifyNote: Distinct: no catalogue page covers separation or partitioning. central-limit-theorem only shows that sums of random steps are Gaussian, and reaction-rates-equilibrium shows forward and reverse rates, not differential migration or band broadening. Level 3 is honest because van Deemter plate height and resolution are taught in undergraduate analytical and instrumental chemistry (Bates, UML and UF lecture notes; LibreTexts CHM 331 problems). Both prerequisites are level 2, so neither sits above the topic. It is buildable as a real client-side model: the Giddings-Eyring stochastic model has particles hopping between the phases with exponential residence times set by k', plus axial diffusion and multipath, and runs easily at interactive rates. H(u) can be measured from the simulated peak variance and checked against H = A + B/u + Cu. It needs no external data: partition coefficients and diffusivities are generic parameters, not claims about real compounds. Two small accuracy fixes. First, the interaction says eddy paths, longitudinal diffusion and slow exchange 'each take their turn' as the flow changes. In the van Deemter equation the eddy (A) term does not depend on flow; it is a floor set by the packing. Only B/u dominates at low flow and Cu at high flow. Second, the pitfall says the bands are Gaussian because the hopping is random. They are only near-Gaussian, because many random hops add up; real peaks tail, and few exchanges or a heterogeneous surface skew them.

fix.interaction: Inject a mixture at the top of a column and watch each molecule hop at random between the moving phase and the stationary phase. The time each one spends stuck is set by its partition coefficient, so the bands separate and broaden, and a detector at the end draws the chromatogram. Slide the flow rate and the measured plate height traces the van Deemter curve: diffusion along the column dominates at slow flow, slow exchange at fast flow, and the uneven paths through the packing add a floor that the flow does not change. Lengthen the column or use finer packing to see the resolution improve.
fix.pitfall: Most chromatography is not a sieve by size: two molecules of the same size separate because they stick differently. The bands are close to Gaussian only because each molecule makes many random hops that add up; with few exchanges or uneven sticky sites, real peaks tail.
fix.needs: No external data: the model is the Giddings-Eyring stochastic model (exponential residence times in each phase, plus axial diffusion and multipath dispersion), with illustrative partition coefficients and diffusivities, not values for named compounds.

final.title: Dislocations: why metals bend and alloys resist
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Why metals yield far below bond strength is a striking, showable mechanism at the heart of materials science, and no existing page covers it.

build 4: 2D Lennard-Jones molecular dynamics of a few thousand atoms with an edge dislocation glides under shear at interactive rates and shows solute pinning, but convincing work-hardening pile-ups need more atoms than a browser box holds, so that last step should stay modest.
final.verifyNote: Nothing in the catalogue covers dislocations (bridges-structures stays at the scale of members). Level 3 is honest: dislocation glide and solid-solution strengthening are core university materials science (MIT 3.012, MITx 3.012S.3x). A 2D Lennard-Jones crystal of a few hundred to a few thousand atoms is buildable on the client: states-of-matter already runs 2D molecular dynamics, and Bailey, Sethna and Myers simulate an edge dislocation in a 2D Lennard-Jones crystal. Three problems need fixing. (a) The takeaway's 'a thousand times below' cannot be observed in the graphic: a small 2D Lennard-Jones toy shows a large gap, but not the factor of 100 to 10,000 of real metals. The number belongs in the text, not the takeaway. (b) Work hardening by multiplying dislocations needs dislocation sources and large boxes; the honest small-box version is a pile-up against an obstacle. (c) newtons-laws is an unhelpful prerequisite. The crystal lattice comes from semiconductors ('Crystals & semiconductors') and the atom-box simulation from states-of-matter.

fix.interaction: Shear a two-dimensional crystal of simulated atoms that contains an edge dislocation, and watch the defect glide one row of bonds at a time while a gauge shows the stress it took. Remove the dislocation, and the perfect crystal holds to a far higher stress before a whole plane slips at once. Sprinkle in larger or smaller foreign atoms and the dislocation snags on them, so the gauge must climb higher before it moves. Add a second and third dislocation and drive them against a row of obstacles, where they pile up and resist further slip.
fix.takeaway: A crystal with a dislocation yields at a small fraction of the stress a perfect crystal needs, because the defect breaks one row of bonds at a time, and foreign atoms raise that stress by pinning it.
fix.needs: None beyond a 2D Lennard-Jones pair potential, the same kind of model states-of-matter runs. Solute atoms are modelled as particles with a larger or smaller size parameter. The real-metal factor between ideal and measured shear strength (G/10 against measured yield) is quoted in the text from textbook values.
fix.needsSource: none

final.title: Molecular orbitals & conjugation
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Diagonalizing Hückel matrices to explain dye colour and aromaticity is a real model with a visual payoff, and chemical-bonds' VSEPR picture does not cover it.

build 5: Diagonalizing a small Hückel adjacency matrix is exact and instant, the ring and chain level patterns and aromaticity show directly, and the cyanine absorption maxima are published facts; simple Hückel gets only the trend of the gap, not absolute colours, and the page should say so.
final.verifyNote: Distinct: chemical-bonds (L1) uses localized pairs and VSEPR, and the pool's hartree-fock does a different self-consistent method. The level is honest (MIT 5.61 lecture on Hückel), the build is real (diagonalize an N×N matrix of at most about 20 sites in the browser), and the data are just literature λmax facts for a cyanine series, as used in standard undergraduate labs (KIT practical, Rioux). Two small faults. The takeaway ties stability to ring size ('six-membered stable, four-membered not'), but the actual rule is the electron count (4n+2 against 4n): cyclooctatetraene fails too, and charged rings such as C5H5- and C7H7+ pass. The interaction should also say that simple Hückel overestimates how far a polyene's gap closes, which is why the colour panel uses cyanines (bonds evened out) and not long polyenes.

fix.takeaway: Electrons delocalized over a π system fill a ladder of orbitals whose gap narrows as the system grows, which is why longer dyes absorb redder light, and a ring is stabilized only when its π electrons exactly fill a closed shell (2, 6, 10: benzene) and destabilized when they half-fill a degenerate pair (4, 8: cyclobutadiene).
fix.interaction: Snap carbon atoms into chains and rings to build a π system (ethene, butadiene, benzene, cyclobutadiene, the cyclopentadienyl anion, a cyanine dye); the page diagonalizes the Hückel matrix and draws the molecular orbitals as signed lobes on the atoms beside an energy ladder filled with the π electrons. Lengthen a cyanine chain and watch the HOMO-LUMO gap shrink beside the dye series' measured absorption maxima and a swatch of the colour it absorbs; close a chain into a ring and add or remove electrons to see which counts fill a closed shell and which leave two electrons alone in a degenerate pair.

final.title: Catalysis on a surface
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The Ziff-Gulari-Barshad lattice model shows site coverage and CO poisoning, a mechanism the existing page's barrier-lowering catalyst never models.

build 5: The Ziff-Gulari-Barshad lattice model is a classic, cheap cellular simulation whose CO-poisoning transition emerges on its own, and adding desorption with temperature is a one-line extension. It needs no data.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from reaction-rates-equilibrium, whose catalyst only lowers a barrier, and a ZGB lattice Monte Carlo of about 100x100 sites runs easily in the browser; it needs no data. But the interaction misdescribes the ZGB model. The rate does not simply 'rise, peak and collapse as the surface smothers in CO'. Below a CO fraction of about 0.39 the surface is poisoned by oxygen (a continuous transition, rate zero), and the rate climbs across a reactive window before falling abruptly, a first-order jump, to CO poisoning at about 0.525. The 'Langmuir isotherm' alongside is also the wrong comparison: ZGB is a non-equilibrium steady state, so the fair comparison is the mean-field Langmuir-Hinshelwood rate, which misses the poisoning transitions the lattice shows. Small fix to the interaction; the takeaway already allows either reactant to poison.

fix.interaction: Run CO oxidation on a lattice of catalyst sites: CO lands on one empty site, O2 splits onto two neighbouring empty sites, and adjacent CO and O react into CO2 and leave (the Ziff-Gulari-Barshad model). Slide the CO fraction in the gas: with too little CO the surface fills with oxygen and goes dead, across a narrow window the CO2 rate climbs, and just past its peak it collapses abruptly as CO covers every site, with the lattice's rate and coverages plotted beside the smooth mean-field Langmuir-Hinshelwood prediction that misses both dead ends. Add a CO desorption rate (a hotter surface) and watch the abrupt collapse soften and the poisoned surface recover.

final.title: Reaction trajectories & the transition state
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Classical trajectories on a LEPS surface with Polanyi's early/late barrier rules and the kinetic isotope effect are the real university model behind the 1D profile on reaction-rates-equilibrium.

build 5: Classical trajectories on a LEPS surface for H+H2 and F+H2 are a textbook small ODE with published Sato parameters (facts). Polanyi's early/late barrier rules and Eyring rates follow directly. The zero-point-energy isotope effect must be added as a stated harmonic correction.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from reaction-rates-equilibrium (a 1D profile only), and buildable: collinear A+BC on a LEPS surface is a 2-degree-of-freedom ODE, cheap to integrate live, and LEPS/Sato parameters for H3 and FH2 are published numbers reproduced in teaching labs (for example the Imperial College MRD lab). The level is honest (MIT 5.60). But a purely classical trajectory has no zero-point energy, so the H/D swap as written cannot show a ZPE effect. The trajectories must be quasiclassical (the initial vibration seeded with its ZPE) and the Eyring rate must use a ZPE-corrected barrier, and even then the transition state's ZPE is a known weakness of QCT. 'Move the barrier early or late' also has no honest continuous control on a fixed LEPS surface. The honest version is to compare F+H2 (early barrier), its reverse H+HF (late barrier) and symmetric H+H2.

fix.interaction: Fire a quasiclassical trajectory of A + BC → AB + C across a potential-energy surface (LEPS model of H + H2 and F + H2) drawn as a contour map, choosing how much energy goes into translation and how much into vibration (never less than the zero-point vibration), and see whether it crosses the saddle or turns back. Compare the early barrier of F + H2 with the late barrier of its reverse, H + HF, to see that translation carries molecules over an early pass and vibration over a late one; sweep the temperature to watch the Eyring rate climb, and swap H for D to watch the zero-point energies, the effective barrier and the rate change.

final.title: How ants find the shortest way
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Stigmergy with fading pheromone is a clear emergent mechanism a 10-year-old can run and test (double bridge, evaporation off), and nothing on the site shows it.

build 5: A pheromone-laying and evaporating agent model with the double-bridge experiment is a classic, cheap simulation whose takeaway emerges visibly (shorter bridge wins; no evaporation means lock-in). It needs no data.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from graph-search (no map, agents plus a scent field), honest level 0, and buildable as an agent model with a pheromone grid (NetLogo Ants). The problem is the mechanism. In Deneubourg's and Goss's double-bridge work the short branch wins because ants that take it get back sooner and lay scent on it first, so it pulls ahead even with no fading. Fading matters when a shortcut appears later: Goss et al. 1989 (Naturwissenschaften 76:579) added the short branch after a trail had formed, and the Argentine ants mostly stayed on the long one. So 'with fading switched off the colony stays stuck on whichever bridge it found first' is wrong when both bridges are offered at once, and the takeaway credits the fading for what the round-trip time does. The fix rewrites the interaction and takeaway to separate the two effects.

fix.interaction: Ants wander out of a nest at random; one that finds the sugar walks home laying a scent, and the others tend to follow scent, so a trail forms and thickens. Drag the sugar farther away or drop a pebble on the trail and watch the colony reroute. Then offer a long bridge and a short one together and count the ants on each: ants on the short one get back first, so its scent builds up sooner and the short one wins. Open the short bridge only after a trail has formed on the long one, and the colony stays on the long one until the scent's fading is switched on.
fix.takeaway: A colony finds the shorter path with no map and no ant that knows it: ants on the short route return sooner, so its scent builds up faster and draws more ants, and a fading scent lets the colony give up an old route.
fix.pitfall: No ant knows where the food is or compares the routes, and the queen gives no orders. Fading is not what makes the short bridge win when both are offered at once; it is what lets a colony switch to a shortcut that appears later, and real Argentine ants often do not. Real ants also use sight and memory, which the page leaves out and says so.

final.title: Camouflage: you are the hungry bird
judgeNotes: build 4: The heritable-shade population model with the reader as selective predator is a real, simple genetic model rather than a picture to tap, since the next generation is computed from the survivors; procedural bark avoids licence questions.
fit-level 5: The reader acting as the selective predator makes the mechanism the toy itself, a strong level-0 doorway to evolution that is distinct from that page's slider-driven population.
final.verifyNote: Sound in substance. The model (heritable shade with small variation, plus the reader's own predation) is real and cheap. The takeaway shows in the graphic, and the pitfall is right. The page differs from evolution, where the predator is a slider, because here the reader is the predator. leadsTo evolution and meiosis-inheritance are both existing level-1 pages. The weak point is the 'why': a CliffsNotes page is not a curriculum source. The KS2 Year 6 statutory requirement on adaptation and the NGSS standard should be cited directly.

final.title: Fireflies that flash together
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Pulse-coupled oscillators syncing with one coupling slider is a magical, genuinely model-driven level-0 toy, distinct from resonance and from the flocking and ant emergence pages.
build 5: Mirollo-Strogatz pulse-coupled integrate-and-fire oscillators on a 2D field are cheap and honest, and synchrony visibly emerges as the single coupling slider rises. It needs no data.
final.verifyNote: No existing page shows pulse-coupled synchronization. oscillations-resonance is one driven oscillator, and the pool's kuramoto-synchronization is the level-3 phase model, so this is the level-0 entry to it. The model is a pulse-coupled integrate-and-fire population (Mirollo-Strogatz, as in Nicky Case's explorable), which runs easily in the browser with one coupling control, and the synchrony is visible without text. Needs no data. The takeaway and pitfall are sound: there is no leader, and only some species (Photinus carolinus, Pteroptyx) do this. The leadsTo link to oscillations-resonance is loose but acceptable.

final.title: Flocks without a leader
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Boids' three rules, switched off one at a time, is the canonical emergent-behaviour toy, wordless and formula-free, with no counterpart on the site.
build 5: Reynolds boids with switchable separation/alignment/cohesion rules and a predator is a classic, small agent simulation in which each rule's effect is directly observable. It needs no data.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from ecosystems (population counts, not movement) and buildable: boids run in the browser at interactive rates, at an honest level 0, with NGSS 3-LS2-1 as the signal. The fault is factual. The takeaway says real flocks keep their shape 'because every bird follows the same three simple rules'. Reynolds's three rules are a model that reproduces flocking, not measured bird behaviour. Field data (Ballerini et al. 2008, PNAS) show starlings each track a fixed count of about six or seven nearest neighbours, whatever the distance. The takeaway should say the rules are sufficient, not that they are what birds do, and the pitfall can name the measured neighbour count.

fix.takeaway: A flock can hold together and turn as one with no leader: in the model, three simple rules about each bird's nearest neighbours are enough to make one.
fix.pitfall: No bird leads or sees the whole flock, and the three rules are a model that reproduces flocking, not a list real birds were found to obey. Real starlings each keep track of about six or seven nearest neighbours, however far apart they are (Ballerini et al. 2008), and nobody plans the shapes of a murmuration.

final.title: Diffusion, osmosis & active transport
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A core GCSE topic missing from the catalogue, with particle-level mechanisms the graphic shows naturally (spreading, membrane, swelling cell, pump); entropy's mixing count and the-cell's structure do not cover it.

build 4: A 2D particle box with a membrane that passes only solvent particles is a real model and close to the existing states-of-matter engine; diffusion, osmotic flow and a pump that spends ATP all come out of it, though the scope (four scenes) is large, and in 2D the water level has to be shown as a movable partition or the compartment's volume, not as true hydrostatic height.
final.verifyNote: Distinct enough: entropy mixes two gases with no membrane, the-cell is structure, and the pool's level-0 smells-and-diffusion has no membrane, no osmosis and no pump. The level-1 rating is honest (AQA GCSE 4.1.3), the prerequisites are level 1, and a particle box with a membrane that lets water through and blocks solute is a real client-side model. The flaw is that the takeaway says water 'does the same' as diffusing particles, the textbook story that water flows down its own concentration gradient. That is a known misconception: Kramer and Myers (2013, Trends in Plant Science) show osmotic flow is several times larger than water's diffusion alone would give, and it comes from the solute's push on the membrane. The particle simulation would itself show bulk flow, so the page must not explain it as dilution. The fix keeps the GCSE outcome (water moves toward the side with more dissolved particles) without the false cause.

fix.takeaway: Particles spread from where they are crowded to where they are not by random motion alone; a membrane that holds dissolved particles back makes water flow toward the side with more of them; and moving anything the other way costs energy.
fix.pitfall: Osmosis moves water toward the side with more dissolved particles, but not because those particles 'dilute' the water so that fewer water molecules reach the pore: the flow is far larger than water's own diffusion would give, and it comes from the trapped particles pushing on the membrane. Diffusion needs no force or pump; particles have no direction of their own, and the net flow is a counting effect. A plant cell in pure water becomes firm rather than bursting, because of its wall.

final.title: PCR: copying DNA until there is enough to see
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Its doubling-per-cycle model and the Ct readout are a vivid, real mechanism that everyone met through COVID tests, and it is distinct from dna-to-protein; the PCR-test link fits level 1 well.

build 5: Doubling per cycle, with efficiency falling as primers and nucleotides run out, is a small exact model; the threshold-cycle shift of log2(1000), about ten cycles, comes straight out of it, and primer matching is a simple string test.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from every existing page: dna-to-protein reads a gene, and nothing in the catalogue covers amplification. The pool's dna-fingerprinting uses PCR only as one step. The model (doubling per cycle, logistic depletion of primers and nucleotides, threshold crossing) is small and real. The quoted numbers check out: at 100% efficiency each tenfold dilution adds about 3.32 cycles, so 1 copy versus 1000 copies is about 10 cycles, and 2^30 is about 1e9. The pitfall is sound: the plateau carries no information about the starting amount, and Ct tracks the amount of template, not how ill someone is. Level 1 is honest (A-level and IB biology teach PCR, and the doubling arithmetic is high-school level). No external data is needed. Small fix: the exact target-length fragment only appears from cycle 3, so the page should not draw the first doublings as already target-sized copies.

fix.pitfall: Doubling is not forever: primers and nucleotides run out and the curve flattens, so the plateau says nothing about the starting amount; only the threshold cycle does. A Ct value is not a measure of how ill someone is. Nor is every copy the target from the first cycle: the short piece bounded by both primers only appears from the third cycle, after which it dominates.

final.title: Bacterial chemotaxis
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A textbook university systems-biology model (run-and-tumble, Barkai-Leibler perfect adaptation) whose emergent drift up the gradient is exactly what an animated simulation shows best, and no page is like it.

build 5: A few hundred run-and-tumble agents, each running a small ODE for receptor methylation with exact adaptation, run comfortably in real time, and the drift up the gradient and the dip-and-recover under a uniform dose come out of the model itself.
final.verifyNote: No existing page shows run-and-tumble or adaptation. ecosystems and homeostasis are unrelated mechanisms. A few hundred agents, each with a reduced Barkai-Leibler (receptor activity plus methylation) state, runs easily at interactive rates. Perfect adaptation after a uniform step, with tumble frequency recovering within seconds, is the established result (Barkai & Leibler 1997; Alon et al. 1999). The takeaway is observable in the drifting swarm and the dip-and-recover trace, and the pitfall is correct. Level 3 is honest: university systems-biology courses (Alon's Introduction to Systems Biology, MIT 7.32/8.591) teach it. No external data is needed beyond published rate constants. Small improvement: the pool's random-walks page should be a related link.

final.title: Gene regulation & the lac operon
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The canonical model of gene regulation (Ozbudak et al.), with hysteresis and diauxie the toy shows, and it is the prerequisite other candidates rely on; it is distinct from dna-to-protein, and its prerequisite reaction-rates-equilibrium is at level 2, which suits level 3.

build 4: The Ozbudak-style bistable ODE gives the hysteresis loop honestly; showing the diauxic pause needs a separate growth-and-substrate model (Monod with catabolite repression) coupled to it, which is small but should be stated.
final.verifyNote: The topic is distinct and buildable: a small ODE (Ozbudak 2004 or Santillán-style) from published parameters, with no external data. The pool's genetic-circuits page shows synthetic toggle switches, while this one is the natural two-signal operon and diauxie. Two parts of the interaction overstate the textbook picture, though. (a) It says to sweep 'the inducer' up and down for hysteresis, but the pitfall itself notes bistability was measured with TMG and not shown with lactose (Ozbudak et al. 2004, and later reviews), so the sweep must be explicitly with a gratuitous inducer. (b) It attributes glucose's effect to CAP alone, but in E. coli the glucose-lactose diauxie is mainly caused by inducer exclusion: unphosphorylated EIIA-Glc blocks LacY while glucose is being imported, and cAMP levels barely differ between the two sugars (Inada et al. 1996; Kimata et al. 1997, PNAS). CAP-cAMP plays a supporting role. The overlap with genetic-circuits should also be named.

fix.interaction: Set the glucose and lactose in a bacterium's medium and watch an ODE model of the lac operon respond: the repressor leaves the operator when an inducer is present, the permease the operon makes imports more inducer, and while glucose is flowing in the glucose transporter blocks that permease (inducer exclusion), with CAP-cAMP giving a smaller extra boost when glucose is scarce. Sweep the gratuitous inducer TMG up and then down to trace the hysteresis loop, and grow a culture on both sugars to see the diauxic pause when the glucose runs out.
fix.pitfall: Bistability and hysteresis were measured with the gratuitous inducer TMG; with plain lactose the loop is weak or absent because lactose is also consumed, so the page must not present lactose itself as a memory switch. Nor should it pin the diauxic pause on cAMP and CAP alone: in E. coli it comes mainly from inducer exclusion, where glucose uptake blocks the lactose permease.
fix.overlapWith: dna-to-protein: that page reads one gene into a protein; this one is about when the gene is read at all, as a dynamical switch with feedback (model of Ozbudak et al. 2004). genetic-circuits (pool) builds synthetic switches from parts; this is the natural operon, with two sugar signals and diauxic growth.

final.title: Morphogen gradients & positional information
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Covers the reserve item on pattern formation with a real diffusion-decay model and the French flag; it is distinct, but it should be planned together with turing-patterns and segmentation-clock so the three do not blur.
build 5: A 1D diffusion-decay PDE with thresholds is a small honest model with an analytic steady state to check against; the scaling mechanism needs one stated extra term.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from every existing page: the-cell is an organelle zoom and nothing in biology covers development (the catalogue's Reserve list names 'Embryo development & pattern formation' as missing). The selected turing-patterns page is a different mechanism (self-organised wavelength, no source), so the two make a natural pair rather than a duplicate. Level 3 is honest: the steady-state synthesis-diffusion-degradation profile, length scale sqrt(D/k), thresholds and positional error are university developmental and systems biology material. Prerequisites the-cell and dna-to-protein are level 1. It runs as a 1D reaction-diffusion PDE, cheap in the browser. The pitfall is accurate, since Bicoid gradient formation is still debated. The one vague point is 'switch on a scaling mechanism'. The literature model is Ben-Zvi and Barkai's expansion-repression circuit (an expander that widens the gradient and is repressed by morphogen signalling), which also runs as a small PDE. The fix names that model, makes the noise step compute positional error from the gradient's slope, and links turing-patterns.

fix.interaction: Drag the production rate, diffusion constant and lifetime of a morphogen made at one end of a row of cells and watch its concentration profile settle into an exponential whose length scale, the square root of diffusion over decay, the page reports. Set two or three thresholds and the cells paint themselves in bands, Wolpert's French flag. Double the tissue's length and the bands fail to scale; switch on Ben-Zvi and Barkai's expansion-repression circuit (a second diffusing 'expander' that widens the gradient and is shut off by the morphogen) and the bands stay in proportion. Add noise to the concentration and see that boundaries where the gradient is steep stay sharp while those in its flat tail blur.
fix.needs: No data needed: a 1D synthesis-diffusion-degradation PDE plus the expansion-repression model (Ben-Zvi & Barkai 2010, PNAS), both run live. Optional comparison: published Bicoid length scales (about 20% of egg length, Gregor et al. 2007), quoted as numbers with citation.
fix.needsSource: none (model only; quoted literature values cited, not redistributed)

final.title: Population genetics: drift & selection
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Wright-Fisher drift versus selection, with Kimura's fixation probability, is the core university model the evolution page lacks, and it is ideal for many live traces.
build 5: A hundred Wright-Fisher binomial traces per generation are cheap, and fixation near 2s and the Hardy-Weinberg ratios are exact checks; no data needed.
final.verifyNote: The topic is distinct from evolution (an explicit allele with N and s, and drift kept apart from selection). The Wright-Fisher model is binomial sampling, trivially fast for a hundred populations, and level 3 is honest (university population genetics, per the cited syllabus). It has two factual errors. (1) The interaction says the counter shows how often a beneficial mutation is lost, 'approaching Kimura's 2s', but 2s is the probability of fixation, not of loss (Haldane 1927, generalized by Kimura). (2) The takeaway says most beneficial mutations are lost because the population is small, but a new beneficial mutation fixes with probability about 2s whatever N is (once Ns >> 1), so even in a huge population most are lost by chance while still rare. Small N makes drift dominate selection: that is the regime where |Ns| is about 1 or less.

fix.interaction: Run a hundred Wright-Fisher populations at once as allele-frequency traces: with no selection they wander and fix at random, faster in small populations; with a selection coefficient s they bend toward fixation, and a counter shows the share of new beneficial mutations that fix, approaching Haldane's 2s however large the population, so most are lost anyway. Set dominance to see recessive alleles hide from selection, and compare the Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies with the simulated ones each generation.
fix.takeaway: Allele frequencies change by chance as well as by selection: in a small population chance can fix a harmful allele or lose a good one, and even in a large population most new beneficial mutations vanish while they are still rare.

final.title: Turing patterns
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Reaction-diffusion spots and stripes are a beautiful, widely sought mechanism driven by a real PDE, and they are distinct from chaos-fractals.

build 5: A Gierer-Meinhardt or Gray-Scott grid PDE runs at interactive rates in JS (or WebGL) and shows the diffusion-ratio threshold honestly; growing and tapered domains are a mask on the same grid.
final.verifyNote: Nothing in the catalogue runs a reaction-diffusion PDE. chaos-fractals iterates maps, and morphogen-gradients and segmentation-clock are separate pool proposals. A 2D activator-inhibitor grid (Gierer-Meinhardt or Schnakenberg) runs at interactive rates on the client. Level 3 is honest: Turing instability and its diffusion-ratio condition are taught in university mathematical biology (Murray).
