The diffusion-ratio threshold, the stripes inserted as the domain grows (Kondo & Asai 1995, Pomacanthus) and the spots that turn to bands on a tapering tail are standard results, and the pitfall about contested cases is sound. Two small corrections. The wavelength is set by the reaction rates together with the two diffusion coefficients, not by 'rates alone'. The angelfish case is itself debated (Painter, Maini & Othmer 1999 add cell movement), so the pitfall should hedge it.

fix.takeaway: Two chemicals, one that makes more of itself and a faster-spreading one that suppresses it, can turn a uniform field into regular spots or stripes with no blueprint, at a spacing set by their reaction and diffusion rates.
fix.pitfall: Not every stripe in nature is a Turing pattern. The page should name where a Turing-type mechanism is well supported (digit spacing, hair and feather follicles) and where the evidence is mixed (fish skin, where pigment cells also move). It must not claim the mechanism for zebra stripes or fingerprints without saying that is contested.

final.title: How your ear hears
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Promotes the reserve cochlea item as a clear place-by-pitch mechanism with one slider, distinct from waves-interference's wave in the air.

build 4: The Greenwood place function with a bank of passive resonators along the basilar membrane, driven by the tone, computes the bump positions honestly and runs easily; the ossicle lever is a stated gain.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from waves-interference (the wave in air) and vision-color; acceptable alongside the proposed level-0 vibrations-and-sound (source and medium, no ear) and level-3 cochlea-hearing (active amplifier, implants), though those should be related. Level 0 is honest and a passive tuned-filter bank on the Greenwood map is a real, cheap model. But the middle-ear mechanism as written is a known textbook misconception: the ossicles' lever gives only about 1.3x; most of the gain (around 13-20x, roughly 25 dB) comes from the eardrum's large area pushing on the tiny stirrup footplate (Britannica; Wikipedia 'Middle ear'). 'Three tiny bones lever the shake' and a needsSource of 'a middle-ear lever ratio' would teach the wrong thing. Also loudness does not only grow the bump: loud tones broaden it and shift it slightly, so the pitfall should say 'mainly'.

fix.interaction: Slide a tone from low to high and watch it shake the big eardrum, which passes the shake through three tiny bones onto a much smaller window into the fluid of the snail-shaped cochlea, concentrating the push; a ripple then runs along the cochlea's ribbon until it peaks at one spot. Each pitch peaks somewhere else, high notes near the entrance and low notes at the far end. Play two notes at once and see two bumps; turn the loudness up and the bumps grow.
fix.needsSource: none: the Greenwood (1961) frequency-to-place function for the human cochlea, the middle ear's eardrum-to-footplate area ratio (about 17 to 1) with a small ossicle lever (about 1.3), and a passive bank of tuned filters for the ribbon, stated as a simplification
fix.pitfall: The cochlea is not a microphone with one signal: it is thousands of sensors each listening at its own spot. Loud is not the same as high: loudness mainly grows the bump, pitch moves it. And the little bones are not the main amplifier: most of the boost comes from a big eardrum pushing on a tiny window.

final.title: Muscles pull in pairs
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Antagonistic pairs plus the elbow lever (the biceps pulls many times the load) is a vivid mechanism readable with counts and comparisons only, and nothing existing shows it.
build 5: A two-link lever with real attachment distances gives the roughly tenfold biceps force directly; a clear, small, honest statics model whose result can be read off the graphic.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from bridges-structures and from the proposed joints-and-skeleton (joint shapes, no forces); it overlaps the proposed levers-and-scissors only in the lever ratio, which here is applied to the body, so acceptable with a related link. Level 0 and the two-link statics model are honest; the force ratio is right (biceps inserts about 4-5 cm from the elbow, hand about 35 cm, so roughly 7-8 times the load with the forearm level). But the interaction teaches a common misconception: dragging the hand down with a bag in it is not the triceps' job; the biceps keeps pulling while it lengthens to lower the load slowly (an eccentric contraction), and gravity does the lowering. The triceps straightens the elbow against resistance (pushing up from a chair, pushing down on a table, lifting the hand overhead). The page must show this or it repeats the error the pitfall claims to avoid.

fix.interaction: Drag the hand of a cutaway arm: bending the elbow, the biceps shortens and bulges; straightening it against a push, such as pressing down on a table or pushing up from a chair, the triceps shortens instead, and tugging either muscle alone shows it can only pull, never push. Hang a bag of shopping from the hand and watch the biceps pull many times the bag's weight, because it grips the forearm so close to the elbow; lower the bag slowly and the biceps is still the one pulling, getting longer as it lets the bag down.
fix.pitfall: Muscles never push; the opposite movement is another muscle pulling, or gravity. Lowering a bag slowly is the biceps braking while it lengthens, not the triceps pushing it down. And a bigger muscle does not change the lever: it still pulls from the same place.

final.title: Why spinning makes you dizzy
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Lagging fluid in the semicircular canals, and the reversed feeling on stopping, is a clean inertia mechanism every child has felt, and no existing page covers it.

build 5: The torsion-pendulum canal model with a time constant of a few seconds plus velocity storage is the standard model, a one-line ODE driven by the slider, and the reversed sensation after stopping emerges from it directly.
final.verifyNote: Distinct: no catalogue page covers the vestibular system (the related L0 candidate hearing-and-the-ear covers the cochlea, not the canals). The torsion-pendulum model of the canal (cupula lag, ~7-10 s return during steady spin, reversed deflection on stopping) is the textbook mechanism and runs trivially in the browser with one slider. Takeaway is visible in the graphic, and the pitfall is correct. Honest L0: no formulas, one control, starts from a familiar experience. Small fix: it is an everyday experience, and the related link to oscillations-resonance should be mutual through leadsTo, which it already is.

final.title: Why you get sleepy
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The two-process model (a sleep-pressure tank plus a circadian window) is a real model that works as a level-0 toy with one bedtime control, high in everyday interest and distinct from homeostasis.

build 5: Borbely's two-process model (exponential Process S, sinusoidal Process C, two thresholds) is a published, tiny model that runs instantly and shows sleep deprivation and nap effects without text; the ninety-minute stage strip is an honest stylisation.
final.verifyNote: Distinct and buildable (Borbely two-process model, no data needed; the L3 pool candidate circadian-clocks handles the gene loop), but the pitfall is factually wrong: a weekend lie-in does shift the clock, because late waking moves light exposure, meals and activity later and delays the circadian rhythm; that delay is what social jet lag is (Roenneberg). The fixed-clock two-process model cannot show this, so the page must not claim it. The 90-minute sleep-stage strip is a stylised schedule, not part of the model, and should be labelled as such.

fix.pitfall: The page explains when you get sleepy, not why animals sleep at all, which is still an open question. And the body clock is not fixed: late mornings and evening screen light push it later, which is why a weekend of lie-ins makes Monday feel like jet lag (the toy keeps the clock fixed, and says so).
fix.interaction: Set a bedtime and a wake-up time and run three days: a sleep-pressure tank fills while you are awake and drains while you sleep, and a body clock sets the hours when sleep comes easily; sleepiness is the gap between them. Skip a night and watch the tank overflow; nap in the afternoon and see tonight's sleep come later. A strip under the plot sketches the night's usual rounds of light and deep sleep, about ninety minutes each.

final.title: Pharmacokinetics & dosing
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Accumulation to steady state over four to five half-lives is a widely useful mechanism that needs only exponentials, so it reads more honestly at level 2, and it should absorb liver-drug-metabolism.
build 5: One- and two-compartment models with superposed doses are closed-form or trivial ODEs, and parameters from FDA labels on DailyMed are public domain.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from homeostasis (insulin by hand against a glucose loop) and radioactivity (single exponential decay, no accumulation), and a real buildable compartment ODE. At the judged level 2 (prerequisite calculus is level 2, fine), the interaction is too heavy and the takeaway is overstated: 'whatever the dose' and the pitfall's 'doubling the dose doubles the level' hold only for linear (first-order) elimination, which the page itself breaks with the saturable-elimination switch. The two-compartment option is extra for level 2. Data source: DailyMed's labels are manufacturer-authored and its public-domain status is only asserted secondhand. The openFDA drug-label API (CC0) is the cleaner citation, and the few numeric PK parameters are facts anyway. Overlaps partly with the L3 pool candidate liver-drug-metabolism (first-pass extraction), which this page does not model.

fix.interaction: Place doses on a timeline from a palette (an injection, a tablet, a steady drip, a loading dose) and run them through a one-compartment model whose clearance, volume of distribution and absorption rate are sliders; the blood level is plotted against the drug's therapeutic window. Change the interval, miss a dose or halve the clearance to model a failing kidney, and watch the level, the time to steady state and the peaks and troughs respond; a last switch makes elimination saturable and shows the rules break.
fix.takeaway: Repeated doses pile up until elimination balances intake, and for most drugs that steady state arrives after about four or five half-lives whatever the dose, so the dose sets the level and the half-life sets how long it takes to get there.
fix.pitfall: Doubling the dose of a normally eliminated drug doubles the steady-state level but does not reach it any sooner; only a loading dose shortens the wait. For drugs with saturable elimination (phenytoin, alcohol) neither rule holds.
fix.needs: Clearance, volume of distribution and half-life for four or five example drugs, taken from their US prescribing information.
fix.needsSource: openFDA drug label API (FDA, CC0 1.0): https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/label/ ; the same labels are viewable on DailyMed (https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/). The few numeric parameters are facts, not copyrightable.

final.title: The cerebellum & motor learning
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Visuomotor rotation, with the reader's own hand fitted by the two-rate error-driven model and showing aftereffects and savings, is a real research model and an unforgettable interactive with no overlap.

build 5: Visuomotor rotation measured from the reader's own pointer, with the Smith-Shadmehr two-rate model fitted beside it, is a real experiment plus a tiny published model; aftereffect and savings emerge, and the VOR extension is optional.
final.verifyNote: Distinct (no motor-learning page; reinforcement-learning and gradient-descent are different), buildable (the reader's own cursor reaches under a rotation, plus the Smith-Ghazizadeh-Shadmehr 2006 two-rate state-space model, open access), and honestly level 3. Two factual problems. First, with a 30-degree rotation much of the early, fast correction is deliberate re-aiming, not cerebellar adaptation (Taylor, Krakauer & Ivry 2014), so 'the cerebellum learns' is wrong as a description of the reader's whole curve. Second, the two-rate model predicts savings ('adapt again and learn faster') only after a brief counter-adaptation, not after full washout; its signature prediction is spontaneous recovery. Fix: name the explicit part, show the implicit aftereffect, and use the model's real prediction.

fix.interaction: Move the mouse or a finger to targets while the cursor is secretly rotated by thirty degrees, and watch yourself miss, correct and adapt over a few dozen reaches; beside the hand, a two-rate error-driven model (a fast and a slow learner) updates its prediction trial by trial and its curve sits over the reader's own. Remove the rotation and say 'aim straight': the aftereffect that remains is the implicit, cerebellar part. Reverse the rotation briefly, then hide the errors, and both the model and the hand drift back toward the first adaptation as the fast learner fades and the slow one remains.
fix.takeaway: An implicit learner nudges its prediction a little after every miss, and the aftereffect that survives being told the world is back to normal shows a correction that was learned, not reasoned.
fix.pitfall: Not all of the reader's correction comes from the cerebellum: much of the quick early improvement under a large rotation is deliberate re-aiming, and only the slow, implicit part persists as an aftereffect when the reader is told the rotation is gone.

final.title: Hearing & the cochlea
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The site has no hearing page; the place code (a travelling wave on a graded membrane) and the cochlear-implant finale make a strong, visual, distinct level-3 mechanism.

build 4: A frequency-domain 1D transmission-line cochlea and a band vocoder (Web Audio) for the implant are both cheap. The outer-hair-cell gain is a phenomenological negative damping and should be stated as one. A CC0 speech clip is easy to find.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from vision-color, waves-interference and the L0 candidate hearing-and-the-ear: this page has the active outer-hair-cell amplifier, the audiogram and the implant vocoder. The 1D transmission-line cochlea and a noise vocoder both run in the browser with Web Audio. Prerequisites are levels 1 and 2, so the level is honest. The pitfall (losing outer hair cells removes the amplification, so soft sounds vanish while loud ones still hurt, i.e. recruitment) is well supported. Fixes: the 'why' signal is weak, since place theory is not KS3 content, so cite a university course instead. Noise damage typically shows first as a dip around 4 kHz, not at the extreme base. Name a real open speech source: LibriSpeech is CC BY 4.0, not CC0.

fix.why: MIT OCW HST.720 Physiology of the Ear covers cochlear mechanics and cochlear amplification as core sessions: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/hst-720-physiology-of-the-ear-fall-2004/
fix.interaction: Play a tone, a chord or a spoken word into a cochlea modelled as a chain of coupled resonators whose stiffness falls along the basilar membrane, and watch the travelling wave peak at a place that depends on frequency. Drag the frequency and the peak moves; switch on the outer hair cells' amplification and the peak sharpens; kill the outer hair cells at the place tuned near 4 kHz, as loud noise does, and the audiogram develops the classic notch. Then replace the cochlea with a cochlear implant: split the sound into a few bands, drive one electrode per band, and hear the result.
fix.needs: A short openly licensed speech clip for the implant demonstration (a LibriSpeech utterance, CC BY 4.0, or synthesized speech); the cochlear model itself is a standard one-dimensional transmission-line model with published parameters.
fix.needsSource: LibriSpeech, CC BY 4.0 (https://www.openslr.org/12), or speech synthesized in the browser; no other data

final.title: The ECG & arrhythmias
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Computing the ECG from an excitable-medium model and breaking it into a spiral wave goes far past heart-circulation's synced trace, and it is a showcase mechanism at an honest level 3.

build 4: Aliev–Panfilov on a grid of about 150 by 150 runs spiral waves at interactive rates, a dipole projection gives an honest ECG, and MIT-BIH is ODC-By (verified on PhysioNet). Putting a conduction system and AV node on a 2D sheet is a hand-built approximation and should be presented as one.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from heart-circulation, whose ECG is a drawn P-QRS-T template (circulation.ts) with no tissue model, re-entry or fibrillation. Level 3 is honest because cardiac excitable-media modelling is a biomedical-engineering topic, and all prerequisites are level 1 or 2. It is buildable: a 2D Aliev-Panfilov grid runs explicitly in the browser (an ibiblio e-notes HTML5 demo runs 512x512), and a ~150x150 grid with a pseudo-ECG computed from the dipole is light. The MIT-BIH data is confirmed as ODC-By 1.0 on PhysioNet. Two problems, both small. (1) The takeaway overstates: not every dangerous rhythm is re-entry. Complete heart block (too slow), triggered activity and torsades also exist, and some fast rhythms come from a focus that fires too often. (2) The interaction implies real limb leads from a whole heart. A 2D sheet gives a pseudo-ECG from the net dipole, so it should say so, so the reader doesn't take the simulated trace for a clinical 12-lead. The pitfall is correct.

fix.takeaway: An ECG is the shadow of a wave of excitation crossing the heart, and the most dangerous fast rhythms are usually not a faster pacemaker but a wave that finds a loop and chases its own tail.
fix.interaction: Run a sheet of heart muscle as an excitable medium (the Aliev–Panfilov equations on a grid) with a pacemaker, a fast conduction path and a slow atrioventricular node, and read a pseudo-ECG off it: the tissue's net electrical vector projected onto the three limb leads of Einthoven's triangle. Then break it: slow conduction in a patch, add a scar, fire an early beat into tissue that has only partly recovered and watch a spiral wave take over the trace as tachycardia and then break up into fibrillation; deliver a shock that excites every cell at once and lets the pacemaker take back control. Real annotated recordings from the MIT-BIH database sit beside the simulated traces for comparison.
fix.pitfall: A defibrillator does not restart a stopped heart: it stops a chaotic rhythm so the natural pacemaker can take over, and a flat line is not a shockable rhythm. And not every arrhythmia is re-entry: a heart can also beat too slowly when conduction is blocked.

final.title: MRI: an image from spinning protons
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: medical-imaging only sketches MRI; the Bloch equations, the gradients and filling k-space make a distinct, visually striking level-3 page built on fourier-transform.

build 5: Bloch precession for the signal and a 2D FFT of an analytic Shepp–Logan phantom (line-by-line k-space filling and masking) are small, exact and fast; OpenNeuro data are CC0 if a real slice is wanted.
final.verifyNote: Partly duplicated, and the overlapWith is inaccurate. medical-imaging does not just sketch MRI at the end. It has three full MRI steps (src/routes/medical-imaging/steps.ts): Larmor precession; a gradient whose received signal is Fourier-transformed into a water profile (gradientEcho in imaging.ts, which is exactly 'the signal is the image's Fourier transform' in 1D); and T1/T2 contrast with TR/TE sliders (spinEcho). Its notes even mention k-space. So this candidate's T1/T2 sliders, 'echo time turns fat bright or dark' and the 1D-gradient-equals-Fourier step repeat that page. What is new: 2D phase and frequency encoding filling k-space line by line, a Bloch-equation spin echo (dephasing and refocusing), and the artefacts from editing k-space (centre only, edges only, skipped lines giving aliasing or ghosts). Narrow the page to those, with medical-imaging as a prerequisite to build on. The pitfall is also misleading: standard 2D MRI does acquire slice by slice (a slice-selective pulse with a gradient), so 'the gradient does not scan slice by slice' is wrong. Level 3 is honest (a BME MRI course), and the Shepp-Logan phantom needs no data.

fix.interaction: Start where Medical imaging stops: one gradient turns position into frequency. Step through a real 2D pulse sequence on a phantom: a slice-selective pulse tips the protons, a phase-encoding gradient gives each row its own twist, and a readout gradient records one line of the slice's 2D Fourier transform. Watch k-space fill line by line beside the image that its inverse transform gives so far. A Bloch-equation view of a few spins shows them fan out and refocus into an echo. Then edit k-space: keep only the centre for a blurred image, only the edges for outlines, skip every other line to fold the image onto itself, or shrink the field of view until the head wraps around.
fix.takeaway: An MRI scanner never measures a picture: gradients give each position its own precession frequency and phase, so every echo is one line of the image's 2D Fourier transform, and the centre of k-space carries the contrast while its edges carry the detail.
fix.pitfall: MRI uses no ionizing radiation, and the image is not proton density alone. A point in k-space is not a pixel: every sample holds information about the whole image, which is why dropping lines blurs or ghosts the whole picture instead of leaving holes.
fix.overlapWith: medical-imaging: that page already shows Larmor precession, a single gradient whose Fourier transform gives a 1D water profile, and T1/T2 contrast from TR and TE; this page adds 2D phase-plus-frequency encoding, the echo, filling k-space line by line, and the artefacts of editing it. nmr-spectroscopy (pool, chemistry, level 3) has the same spins and pulses but no gradients and no image.

final.title: Why clouds form, and why their bottoms are flat
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Following one rising bubble of air explains flat cloud bottoms, cold mountains and the rain shadow with no formulas, an excellent level-0 mechanism distinct from atmosphere-weather's global view.

build 5: A rising parcel with the dry adiabatic lapse rate, the Magnus saturation formula and a moist lapse rate over the mountain (foehn) is the standard textbook model: tiny, exact and right for level 0.
final.verifyNote: It is distinct enough: dew-and-fog (pool L0) cools air by contact, and water-cycle and global-water-cycle cover the cycle and budgets, while this page's mechanism is cooling by rising and expansion, the flat base at the lifting condensation level and the rain shadow. A parcel model with the Magnus formula needs no data, and the level is honest for L0 (counts and comparisons only). The numbers are right: about 10 °C per km dry, and the cloud base drops as humidity rises (about 125 m for each degree between the temperature and the dew point). Two factual faults. (a) The interaction says the bubble's 1 °C per 100 m 'is also why it is colder on a mountain', but the air around a mountain cools by only about 6.5 °C per km on average, so the mountain should not show the parcel's dry rate. (b) The pitfall says clouds are 'not lighter than air', which is muddled: a growing cumulus is buoyant air, warmer and lighter than its surroundings, that happens to carry droplets. The droplets are what is heavier, and they stay up because they fall more slowly than the air rises. The droplets point also overlaps how-rain-forms, so it should be kept brief.

fix.interaction: Drag a bubble of air up from the warm ground: it swells and its thermometer drops about one degree for every hundred metres, until the invisible water it carries turns to droplets and the bubble turns white. Every bubble released from the same ground turns white at the same height, so the clouds have flat bottoms; make the day more humid and the cloud base drops, dry the air and clouds form higher or not at all. A last step blows the bubble over a mountain: it cools as it is pushed up the slope, rains on the side facing the wind, and comes down the far side drier and warmer than it started.
fix.takeaway: Rising air swells and cools, and a cloud appears at exactly the height where the air gets cold enough for its water to turn into droplets, which is why the bottoms of clouds are flat.
fix.pitfall: It is not colder up a mountain because it is farther from the Sun: a few kilometres make no difference to sunlight; the air up there is cold because air that rises expands and cools. Clouds are not made of vapour: they are tiny droplets, each heavier than air, that stay up because they fall more slowly than the rising air beneath them.

final.title: How a wildfire crosses a forest, or stops
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A real percolation model a 10-year-old can run, with a surprising sharp threshold as the takeaway; distinct from epidemics (moving crowd) and the deterministic grid candidates.

build 5: Site percolation on a grid, repeated over many runs to tally crossings near the 0.59 threshold, plus firebreak and wind neighbourhoods, is a small, honest stochastic model that runs fast in the browser.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from epidemics (SIR in a moving crowd) and ecosystems: no catalogue page shows site percolation on a fixed grid. The physics checks out: the site-percolation threshold on the square lattice with four neighbours is about 0.5927, and the NetLogo Fire model shows it. The model is a trivial cellular automaton, needs no data, and the level-0 framing ("six in ten", tallies) holds up. One small correction: the jump is only sharp on a large grid, and the line "which is why thinning and firebreaks work" claims too much about real fire management, so the takeaway is tightened.

fix.takeaway: In a big forest, a fire's chance of crossing does not grow gradually with how many trees there are: it flips from almost never to almost always over a narrow band of density, so removing a few trees or cutting a gap can stop a fire that would otherwise get through.

final.title: Where wind comes from: the sea breeze
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The canonical first explanation of wind, from uneven heating, with a reversal at night; one control (the Sun), and distinct from the rotating globe in atmosphere-weather.

build 4: A coarse 2D Boussinesq convection solver (stable-fluids style) with land and sea of different heat capacity, forced by the Sun's angle, is buildable at interactive rates and gives the reversal honestly, though it is the heaviest solver in this batch.
final.verifyNote: It is distinct from atmosphere-weather (level 2: a globe, Coriolis, cells), and a coarse 2D Boussinesq convection solver runs easily in a browser. The level-0 framing is honest, and the pitfall about buoyancy is correct. But the takeaway claims too much: it says wind in general is air moving from cool to warm. Large-scale winds are steered by Earth's rotation and pressure systems and blow mostly along isobars, which is the very content of atmosphere-weather. The takeaway has to be narrowed to the local, thermally driven breeze. The cited standard is fine: the MS-ESS2-5 clarification mentions air flowing from high to low pressure, and MS-ESS2-6 is about unequal heating.

fix.takeaway: Uneven heating is enough to make a wind: by day air slides in from over the cooler sea to replace the warm air rising over the land, and at night the land cools below the sea and the breeze turns around.
fix.pitfall: Warm air does not rise because heat goes up: it rises because it is lighter than the cooler air around it, which pushes it up. And not every wind is a sea breeze: big weather systems are steered by Earth's spin, which this page leaves out.

final.title: Tsunamis: a wave as long as the ocean is deep
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Speed set by depth (the shallow-water wave), with shoaling over real bathymetry, is a striking and honest level-1 mechanism with high public demand; distinct from earthquakes.

build 5: The 1D shallow-water equations on an ETOPO 2022 transect (public domain) are a textbook small PDE that runs at interactive rates, and the speed √(gh), the shoaling and the travel times are real outputs; the stated upper-bound caveat for one transect is honest.
final.verifyNote: No existing page covers tsunamis. earthquakes shows seismic waves inside the Earth. waves-interference shows superposition and standing waves, not depth-limited speed or shoaling. The pool's beach-waves (L0) is wind waves breaking. Level 1 is honest: speed = sqrt(g*depth) is high-school algebra, and the prerequisites (waves-interference L1, earthquakes L1) are not above it. A linear 1D shallow-water solver on a few thousand cells of an ETOPO transect runs at interactive rates, and the entry honestly flags the 1D upper bound. NCEI metadata says ETOPO 2022 is not subject to copyright and may be redistributed at no cost. The takeaway (about 765 km/h over 4,600 m, per NOAA) and the pitfall (flood-like arrival, frequent drawback, not tidal) are correct.

final.title: The carbonate-silicate thermostat
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A genuine level-3 Walker-Hays-Kasting box model coupled to energy balance, with faint-Sun and snowball experiments; distinct from the fast carbon cycle over decades.
build 5: The Walker-Hays-Kasting weathering feedback with a one-layer energy balance is a two-variable ODE box model that integrates over millions of years in milliseconds and needs no data.
final.verifyNote: It is distinct from carbon-cycle (L1: the fast cycle and human emissions over decades) and greenhouse-effect (L1: energy balance, no weathering feedback). The Walker-Hays-Kasting box model with a one-layer energy balance is a small ODE and easily client-side, needing no data beyond published parameters (such as the ~17.7 K e-folding temperature). Level 3 is honest: the topic is taught in graduate and upper-level climate courses (MIT 12.842, UChicago GEOS 32060), and the prerequisites are both L1. The takeaway and pitfall are sound. The page should still call the faint-young-Sun resolution the leading explanation, since higher early CO2 is debated alongside other factors. The weak point is the 'why' signal: it admits the course week was unconfirmed, so replace it with the MIT OCW 12.842 lecture, which covers this exact content.

fix.why: MIT OCW 12.842 Climate Physics and Chemistry, Lecture 4 'The Faint Young Sun Paradox, the geochemical C cycle and climate on geologic time scales': https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/12-842-climate-physics-and-chemistry-fall-2008/resources/part1_lec4
fix.pitfall: This thermostat works over hundreds of thousands to millions of years and does nothing about fossil-fuel CO2 on human timescales; the fast carbon cycle and the slow one are different pages. It is the leading explanation of the faint young Sun paradox, not a settled one: the page should not present a single CO2 history as known.

final.title: Weather forecasts: why they come as odds
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A real mechanism (Lorenz-96 ensembles, spread against error, and the assimilation cycle) that people meet every day in forecasts; it starts where chaos-fractals stops and is honestly university atmospheric science.

build 5: Lorenz-96 with 40 variables is cheap enough that fifty RK4 members plus a small ensemble Kalman filter run easily in the browser; the model is the standard testbed forecasters use and needs no data.
final.verifyNote: The page is distinct and buildable. chaos-fractals (L2) only shows divergence. A 40-variable Lorenz-96 with a 50-member ensemble and an ensemble Kalman filter runs easily in the browser, and data assimilation is university atmospheric-science material, with prerequisites at L2. But the takeaway overstates: a single forecast is not 'useless past a week or so'. Operational deterministic skill reaches about 10 days in midlatitudes, and the intrinsic limit is about two weeks. Synoptic error-doubling estimates range from about 1.5 to 5 days, so 'a couple of days' is acceptable. The pitfall also muddles the probability point: a raw ensemble fraction is exactly a count of members, and calibration is a separate post-processing step. The interaction already shows the real lesson, an over-confident wrong fan from a biased model. Rewrite the takeaway and pitfall.

fix.takeaway: Because small errors in today's weather keep doubling every few days, a single forecast loses its skill after a week or two; forecasters run many from slightly different starts, and where the runs agree the forecast is sure and where they fan out it is not.
fix.pitfall: Chaos does not make forecasting useless: the useful range differs from day to day, and the ensemble shows which days are which. But an ensemble's spread is not automatically a trustworthy probability: a slightly wrong model gives a narrow, confident fan that misses, which is why forecasters check spread against error and calibrate. A '70% chance of rain' means a 70% chance at any one spot, not rain over 70% of the area or 70% of the day.

final.title: Ocean acidification & carbonate chemistry
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Seawater carbonate equilibria with saturation state and the Revelle factor are a real coupled model that acids-bases never reaches; the subject is in high demand and the level is honest.

build 5: Solving the seawater carbonate system with fixed alkalinity is a one-variable root find using published empirical constants (Lueker/Millero/Mucci fits, facts from the literature), which is the honest CO2SYS model and runs instantly.
final.verifyNote: It is distinct from acids-bases (L1 titration and the pH scale) and carbon-cycle (L1 reservoirs and flows). Neither solves the seawater carbonate system or reaches carbonate ion, saturation state or the Revelle factor. Level 3 is honest: it is chemical oceanography with CO2SYS, and the prerequisites (L1 and L2) are not above it. Fixed-alkalinity speciation is a 1D root-find, so the page is instant client-side. The takeaway is correct: polar and cold waters reach aragonite undersaturation first, through higher CO2 solubility and lower alkalinity, and seasonal undersaturation is already observed in some polar seas. The pitfall is correct. Improvement: name the specific published constants, because the needs field is vague. Borate must be included in the alkalinity, or pH comes out wrong.

fix.needs: Published empirical fits for seawater equilibrium constants as functions of temperature and salinity, the same ones CO2SYS uses: K0 (Weiss 1974), K1 and K2 of carbonic acid (Lueker et al. 2000), borate KB (Dickson 1990) and total boron (Uppström 1974) for the alkalinity, and aragonite and calcite solubility (Mucci 1983). These are published coefficients, retyped and cited. Cross-check the solver against PyCO2SYS (open source, GPL-3) in a model test.
fix.needsSource: none beyond published equilibrium-constant fits (Weiss 1974; Lueker et al. 2000; Dickson 1990; Mucci 1983), verified against PyCO2SYS (GPL-3, used only as a test oracle, not shipped)

final.title: Radiative transfer & the climate column
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The emission-height and lapse-rate column is the textbook university step beyond greenhouse-effect's zero-dimensional balance, and it explains stratospheric cooling with the real two-stream model.
build 5: A grey two-stream column with a window band and convective adjustment (Manabe-Wetherald style) is a classic tiny model that relaxes in milliseconds and needs no data.
final.verifyNote: Distinct: the existing greenhouse-effect page (src/routes/greenhouse-effect/climate.ts) is a single leaky-greenhouse layer plus a two-layer ocean energy budget. It has no vertical temperature profile, lapse rate, convective adjustment or emission height. A semi-grey two-stream column with convective adjustment is a standard level-3 model (Pierrehumbert ch. 4) and solves in milliseconds in the browser, with no external data. The takeaway is physically right, with one catch. In a purely grey gas the stratosphere settles at the skin temperature, which does not depend on optical depth, so a grey column will not show stratospheric cooling. Cooling appears only through the infrared window (Goessling and Bathiany's window-grey model, https://esd.copernicus.org/preprints/esd-2016-8/esd-2016-8-manuscript-version4.pdf). Recent work (Cohen, Pincus and Polvani 2026) stresses that it depends on the gas's spectroscopy. The interaction and pitfall should say so, so the page doesn't imply that every greenhouse gas cools the stratosphere.

fix.interaction: A column of air from the surface to the stratosphere, solved with the two-stream radiative transfer equations for a grey gas plus an infrared window, with convection adjusting any layer steeper than the chosen lapse rate. Slide the infrared optical depth (the CO2 amount) and the lapse rate and watch the temperature profile, the tropopause and the emission height move, while a side panel shows which layer the escaping infrared leaves from. Close the window to make the gas fully grey and watch the stratosphere stop cooling as CO2 rises; switch convection off to see pure radiative equilibrium and its unstable lower layers.
fix.pitfall: Greenhouse gases do not trap heat like a lid or reflect infrared; the column warms because the effective emission level rises into colder air. A band that is saturated at the surface still warms the planet, because emission from higher, thinner layers is what matters. Stratospheric cooling is not automatic for any absorber: in a perfectly grey atmosphere the stratosphere's temperature does not change, and it cools here because part of the infrared escapes through the window.

final.title: Comets and their tails
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A clear, surprising mechanism (the Sun blows the tail away, so the comet leaves tail-first) that a 10-year-old can scrub, and it is distinct from orbits-kepler.

build 5: A real Kepler orbit, an anti-sunward ion tail and a dust tail of grains with radiation-pressure beta (the Finson-Probstein particle model) are all small and honest; orbital elements are facts from JPL SBDB/MPC, usable with credit.
final.verifyNote: Distinct (no catalogue page has comets; sun-earth-moon and orbits-kepler never show tails) and an honest L0 toy. A real model is buildable: a Kepler ellipse, a gas tail drawn along the anti-Sun direction, and dust grains released along the orbit with reduced effective gravity (Finson-Probstein syndynes), which produce the lagging curve. Two things need fixing. First, the takeaway says the tail 'always points away from the Sun', but that is exact only for the gas (ion) tail. The page's own dust tail curves and lags behind along the orbit, and from Earth it can even look like an anti-tail pointing sunward. Second, the data licence is left unsettled ('confirm before shipping'). Orbital elements for one or two comets are physical measurements, not creative works, and JPL is a NASA facility whose data are freely reusable with credit, so the source can be stated plainly. Only one real comet is needed, Halley.

fix.takeaway: A comet's tails are pushed out by the Sun, not left behind by its motion, so the gas tail always points straight away from the Sun and the comet leaves tail-first, while the dust tail bends back along the path it has travelled.
fix.needs: Orbital elements of comet 1P/Halley (perihelion distance, eccentricity, period) from the JPL Small-Body Database (https://ssd-api.jpl.nasa.gov/doc/sbdb.html). These are measured physical facts published by NASA/JPL and are freely reusable with the credit 'Courtesy NASA/JPL-Caltech'. Only a few numbers are needed, typed into the model with the credit; no API call happens at runtime. The tail directions come from the model: the gas tail along the anti-Sun line, and dust grains released along the orbit under sunlight pressure.
fix.needsSource: JPL Small-Body Database, Halley's orbital elements (NASA/JPL measured facts, free to reuse with credit)

final.title: Earth is a ball
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: An ideal level-0 page: a familiar experience (the ship hull disappearing first), one drag control, and the 'down means toward the middle' idea that prepares for newtons-laws and sun-earth-moon.

build 4: Horizon distance and hidden height from eye height are an exact geometric construction and the falling ball is trivial radial gravity; it is a small honest model at level 0 and needs no data.
final.verifyNote: Not a duplicate: sun-earth-moon moves a tilted Earth and never shows that it is round or which way is down. The level is honest (NGSS 5-PS2-1 and KS2 Y5 both ask for exactly this), and the model is real sphere geometry: the horizon distance and the height hidden behind it, computed from eye height. Two small improvements keep it honest. Light bending in the air (refraction) lets you see somewhat farther than straight-line geometry predicts (roughly 15% in typical conditions), so the page should not claim exact hull-hiding distances. Also, at true scale the bulge is far too small to see, so the drawing must say the curve is exaggerated. The pitfall 'it doesn't vanish because it got too small' is best shown by a binoculars toggle: zooming in brings back a small ship but not a hidden hull. That makes the takeaway observable without any text.

fix.interaction: Drag a ship out to sea and watch it from the shore. On a flat world it only shrinks, and binoculars bring all of it back. On the round world its hull sinks out of sight before its sails as the sea bulges up between you and it (the curve drawn exaggerated, the distances real). Binoculars cannot bring the hull back, but climbing a cliff can. Then walk a little figure around the globe: wherever it stands its feet point to the middle, and a dropped ball falls toward the middle too, so nobody on the far side falls off.
fix.pitfall: People on the far side are not upside down and do not have to hold on: the page draws no fixed up arrow anywhere. The ship does not vanish because it got too small, and magnifying it does not bring the hull back. The bulge is drawn much bigger than it really is, and air bends light a little so you see slightly farther than the plain geometry says; the page does not claim exact distances.

final.title: Leap years: why February gets an extra day
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Calendar drift is a genuine mechanism, explained with counts of days, that people ask about, and it is distinct from sun-earth-moon's seasons.

build 5: Calendar drift is exact arithmetic of the tropical year (about 365.2422 days, a published constant) against the Julian and Gregorian rules, a clear algorithm whose drift is visible on the wheel.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from sun-earth-moon, which explains why there are seasons, not how a calendar stays lined up with them. It suits L0: it starts from an everyday object (February 29), the numbers are only counts and comparisons (a quarter of a day), and one toggle drives each step. The model is the real arithmetic of the tropical year (about 365.2422 days) against the calendar rules. The numbers check out. Without leap days the calendar slips about 0.24 days a year: roughly a month in about 125 years, and the summer solstice reaches winter after about 750 years ('seven or eight centuries'). The Julian every-four-years rule leaves about one day per 128 years, roughly 8 days in a thousand years, the 'small drift' the 1582 Gregorian reform fixed. The pitfall about 1900 and 2000 is correct. No external data is needed; the length of the year is a standard astronomical constant.

final.title: Interferometry & aperture synthesis
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A genuine level-3 mechanism (uv coverage, dirty beam, CLEAN) built on fourier-transform, and distinct from the single-dish telescopes candidate.
build 5: Baselines tracing uv arcs, a gridded 2D FFT for the dirty beam and image, and Högbom CLEAN on a 128-256 pixel grid are small, exact and fast in the browser, with no data needed.
final.verifyNote: Distinct: no Space page covers telescopes or interferometry; gravitational-waves has a laser interferometer measuring length change, not imaging; medical-imaging is the nearest mechanism (an image computed from indirect samples) but uses projections and back-projection in CT, not Fourier samples from correlated pairs. Level 3 is honest: aperture synthesis is graduate or master's material (NRAO Synthesis Imaging Workshop; Chalmers RRY131; Manchester PHYS40491), and the prerequisites sit at levels 1-2. It can be built in the browser: a 2D FFT on a 128-256 grid, uv tracks from Earth-rotation geometry, and Hogbom CLEAN all run at interactive rates (APSYNSIM, a GPL Python teaching tool, does exactly this on the desktop). The takeaway and pitfall are correct, and so is 'spread it to lose the extended emission': the shortest baseline sets the largest recoverable scale. Small fixes: each baseline samples a Hermitian pair of uv points, not one; name the optional open data (array layouts) in needs; record the medical-imaging contrast in overlapWith.

fix.interaction: Place radio dishes on a map and pick a model sky; every pair of dishes samples the sky's Fourier transform at one point and its mirror image, and as the Earth turns each pair traces a pair of arcs in the uv plane. Watch the dirty beam and the dirty image form from whatever the array has sampled: two dishes see only stripes, a dozen over six hours see the source. Run CLEAN step by step, subtracting the beam from the brightest point until the image emerges, and compare it with the truth; shrink the array to lose resolution, spread it to lose the extended emission.
fix.needs: No external data required: model skies (point sources, a disc, a jet) are generated in code and the model is a 2D FFT plus Hogbom CLEAN. Optional real array layouts (VLA Y with 120-degree arms; ALMA configurations from the CASA simulator's antenna-configuration files, CASA being open source under the GPL), or the coordinates published in open-access papers.
fix.needsSource: none required; optional array layouts from CASA's open-source configuration files (GPL) or open-access papers
fix.overlapWith: light-optics: that page forms images with lenses and never treats resolution as a Fourier limit; medical-imaging also computes an image from indirect measurements, but from projections combined by filtered back-projection, whereas this page fills the Fourier plane with correlations between pairs of separated telescopes and deconvolves with CLEAN.

final.title: The three-body problem & Lagrange points
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The rotating-frame CR3BP with Jacobi zero-velocity curves, tadpole orbits and chaotic divergence is a superb level-3 manipulate page that orbits-kepler does not reach.
build 5: The circular restricted three-body problem in the rotating frame, with Jacobi zero-velocity curves and RK integration of probes, is exact, small and fast.
final.verifyNote: Distinct and honest. orbits-kepler adds a second planet in the inertial frame, while this page uses the rotating frame, the Jacobi constant, zero-velocity curves and the stability of the Lagrange points, which is standard university astrodynamics (MIT OCW 16.346). The circular restricted three-body problem integrates easily in the browser. The takeaway and pitfall need correcting. 'There is no formula for the motion' is too strong: Sundman (1912) found a convergent series solution. The accurate claim is that there is no general closed-form solution and that nearby starts diverge, which is also what the side-by-side probes actually show. The pitfall says the two pulls 'add' at L1 and L2, but at L1 Earth's pull partly cancels the Sun's; only at L2 do they add. The stability of L4 and L5 also depends on the mass ratio: they are stable only below Routh's limit, mu < 0.0385, which Sun-Jupiter, Sun-Earth and Earth-Moon all satisfy. A mass-ratio slider that crosses this limit makes the claim 'two stable points' visible rather than asserted.

fix.interaction: The circular restricted three-body problem, drawn in the frame that rotates with the two large bodies. Set the mass ratio (Sun-Jupiter, Sun-Earth, Earth-Moon, or a slider) and the five Lagrange points appear. Set the probe's energy (the Jacobi constant) and the forbidden regions shade in, opening gates at L1 and L2 as the energy rises. Drop a probe at L1 or L2 and it drifts away within months. Drop one near L4 and it wanders in a tadpole around the point for as long as the reader waits, as Jupiter's Trojans do. Push the mass ratio past about 1 in 26 and the same probe escapes. Nudge a starting position by a hair to run two probes side by side and watch their paths split.
fix.takeaway: Three bodies have no general closed-form solution, and nearby paths split apart, but there are five points where a small body can keep pace: three balanced on a knife edge, two stable while the smaller mass is light enough. An energy map shows where the body can and cannot go.
fix.pitfall: L1 and L2 are not places where gravity cancels. A spacecraft there circles the Sun in exactly one Earth year because the combined pull (Earth's pull partly offsets the Sun's at L1 and adds to it at L2) is exactly what that orbit needs, and it still needs station-keeping. The general three-body problem is not 'unsolvable': Sundman found a convergent series, but no closed formula and no long-term predictability.

final.title: Life on a grid
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Conway's Life is a real, rule-driven mechanism a 10-year-old can paint and run, the toy is the takeaway, and chaos-fractals never shows cellular automata (though leadsTo ecosystems is a weak link; turing-machines or chaos-fractals are not level 1, so consider logic-gates or leave it nearly empty).

build 5: Conway's Life on a small grid with an editable B/S rule is an exact, tiny cellular automaton that steps at thousands of generations a second, and the rule counts can be drawn on each cell; no data needed.
final.verifyNote: No existing page is a cellular automaton (chaos-fractals is L2 with continuous systems, and the Reserve lists cellular automata as a gap). Honest at L0: neighbour counts of 0 to 8, one control at a time, no formulas, and the emerging blinkers and gliders are the takeaway, visible without text. Synchronous Game of Life is an exact, cheap algorithm, needs no data, and has no prerequisites; leadsTo ecosystems is an existing L1 slug (births and deaths from crowding). The pitfall about synchronous update and determinism is correct. Flag for the curator: the pool's cellular-automata (L1, a runner-up) duplicates the Life half of this page and would have to narrow to 1D elementary rules if it were ever promoted.

final.title: Secret codes & code-breaking
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Caesar brute force and frequency analysis are real mechanisms done by counting, a classic primary and middle-school favourite, and clearly distinct from the level-2 cryptography page's key exchange and hashing.
build 5: Caesar brute force and substitution frequency analysis are exact algorithms, and letter counts from a public-domain Project Gutenberg text are freely computable at build time.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from cryptography (L2: key exchange, hashing and signatures), honestly level 0 (letter counts shown as bars), buildable, and its data source is fine (a Project Gutenberg text, public domain). But it overstates frequency analysis: lining up the bars by height finds E, T and A, and nothing more. Past the first few letters the ranks in English are close and change from text to text, so the reader has to fix the rest by spotting part-words. The interaction and takeaway are corrected to say so. leadsTo primes-modular-arithmetic (level 1) is valid.

fix.interaction: Turn the inner ring of a code wheel and type a message: each letter steps along the alphabet by the same amount, and your friend turns the ring back to read it. A spy who does not know the turn tries all 25 turns at once and the one that reads as words jumps out. Scramble the alphabet instead; now the spy counts the letters in the secret message and lines its bars up with the bars of ordinary English: the tallest few give E, T and A, half-words like TH_ appear, and the reader swaps the remaining letters until the message reads.
fix.takeaway: A code that shifts every letter the same way falls to trying all 25 shifts, and a code that scrambles the alphabet falls to counting letters, because in a long message E stays the most common letter however it is disguised.

final.title: Twenty questions: halving the haystack
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Halving against one-by-one search is a core idea shown with counts only, from a game every child knows, and the catalogue has no searching page at all.

build 4: Binary search and a greedy question tree over the UCI Zoo dataset (101 animals, CC BY 4.0 under UCI's repository licence) are exact and tiny; real features will not split exactly in half, which the page must show honestly rather than claim perfect halving.
final.verifyNote: No existing page shows searching by halving. graph-search expands a frontier across a map, and compression (L2) measures bits of surprise with formulas. The counts are right: a number from 1 to 100 takes at most 7 guesses (2^7 = 128), and a 1000-page dictionary about 10 opens. Level 0 is honest (counts only, one question at a time). The UCI Zoo dataset (101 animals, yes/no features) is distributed by UCI under a Creative Commons licence, CC BY 4.0 like UCI's other datasets; the search snippet confirmed Creative Commons but cut off before the version, so the page should cite it with its DOI 10.24432/C5R59V. Its features do not split the animals exactly in half, which is useful: it shows the pitfall honestly. leadsTo sorting and learning-from-data are both level 1. One small fix: the pitfall says halving needs a sorted list, but animal questions need no sorting, only questions that split the pile, so the pitfall now keeps the two cases apart.

fix.pitfall: Halving needs either a list in order (the dictionary trick fails on a shuffled pile of pages) or a question that really splits what is left: show 'is it a penguin?' barely shrinking the board, and do not claim every yes/no question halves the pile.
fix.needsSource: UCI Machine Learning Repository, Zoo dataset (Forsyth 1990, DOI 10.24432/C5R59V), CC BY 4.0.

final.title: How a computer plays a game: the search tree
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Minimax with depth and pruning is a vivid mechanism with a strong visitor draw, honest at level 1 with noughts and crosses and Connect Four, and distinct from graph-search because a value flows up the tree against an opponent.

build 5: Full minimax for noughts and crosses and depth-limited alpha-beta for Connect Four (about 7^6 ≈ 120k nodes at depth 6, fine in a Web Worker) are exact and interactive, with real node counts; no data.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from graph-search (a path through a map, with no opponent and no value passed back up the tree), from reinforcement-learning (values learned in a grid world) and from the pool's monte-carlo-tree-search (random playouts and AlphaGo, level 3). Minimax with alpha-beta pruning runs at interactive rates in a browser: the full noughts-and-crosses tree is tiny, and Connect Four at depth 6 is about 7^6, or 120 thousand positions, fewer with pruning. The facts hold: Connect Four's branching factor is at most 7, and pruning never changes the move chosen. Level 1 is a slight stretch, since alpha-beta usually comes in a first university AI course, but minimax on noughts and crosses is common in high-school computing and the page needs no formulas. One small fix: the 'about sevenfold' figure holds only with pruning off, so the interaction now says that.

fix.interaction: Play noughts and crosses against the page and open its mind: a tree of the moves it is weighing, the leaves scored win, draw or loss and the scores passed up, the computer taking the best of its moves and assuming you take the worst for it. Switch to Connect Four, where the whole tree is too big, and set how many moves ahead it looks: at two it blunders, at six it is hard to beat, and with pruning off the count of positions examined rises about sevenfold per extra move; turn on pruning and watch whole branches greyed out, the count falling steeply with the chosen move unchanged. Build the scoring rule yourself from a palette of features (centre column, three in a row) and test it.

final.title: Caches & the memory hierarchy
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A cache simulator with real parameters, where row against column order changes the miss rate, is a core systems mechanism at the right level, with a strong visual and no overlap with cpu's flat memory.
build 5: A set-associative cache simulator fed by real address traces of row/column sums, a linked-list walk and blocked matrix multiply is exact, fast and produces the hit/miss curves itself.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from cpu (L2), whose memory answers instantly, and from gpu. It is genuinely level 3, covered in MIT 6.004 and in standard computer-architecture courses (Hennessy and Patterson). Buildable as a cache simulator running over address traces generated in the browser; it needs no external data. The facts are right: row-by-row and column-by-column summing differ sharply in miss rate, blocking cuts misses in matrix multiply, a direct-mapped cache thrashes when it alternates between two addresses a cache-size apart, and data moves in whole lines. One small fix: a single miss does cost about the same for one byte as for a whole line, but the takeaway's 'many times faster' should be shown as average memory access time in cycles, not wall-clock speed, so it is observable and honest.

fix.takeaway: The same program, doing the same arithmetic, takes many times more cycles waiting for memory or many times fewer, depending only on whether it touches memory in an order the cache can exploit.

final.title: Hash tables & Bloom filters
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Probe lengths and Bloom false-positive rates, measured against the real formulas, are core data-structure models that suit the site's 'real model' rule, and the page is distinct from cryptography's use of hashes.
build 5: Chaining and open addressing with measured probe lengths, resizing, and a Bloom filter whose measured false-positive rate tracks (1-e^{-kn/m})^k are exact and instant; no data.
final.verifyNote: No existing page covers hashing as an index: cryptography (L2) shows the avalanche of a one-way hash, and sorting covers comparisons, not collisions. The level is honest, since hashing is taught in MIT 6.006 (a second-year CS course), and the prerequisites sorting and binary are both L1. The model is pure algorithm, so it is easily client-side and needs no data. The takeaway and pitfall are correct: a Bloom filter has no false negatives. Small improvement: (1-e^{-kn/m})^k is only the standard approximation. Bose et al. 2008 showed it underestimates the rate, noticeably for small m. The page should say the measured rate tracks it closely for large filters, which a small-bit-array slider can show.

fix.interaction: Insert keys into a table with chaining or open addressing and raise the load factor; every probe is drawn, and the measured mean probe length is plotted against the expected curve until the table resizes and rehashes. Then feed the same keys to a Bloom filter with an adjustable bit array and number of hash functions, query keys that were never inserted and watch the measured false-positive rate track the standard approximation (closely for large arrays, drifting above it for tiny ones); degrade the hash function with a slider and see both structures cluster.

final.title: Barcodes at the checkout
judgeNotes: build 5: A real EAN-13 encoder, decoder and check digit plus a scan-line trace whose widths scale with speed and angle is a small, exact model; the layout is in the public GS1 specification.
fit-level 4: A familiar object with a real mechanism (widths read as ratios, plus a check digit) that a 10-year-old can explore without formulas, distinct from binary and from the QR candidate.
final.verifyNote: No existing page covers barcodes. binary is about bits, and this page is about width patterns, reading by proportion and a check digit. Level 0 is honest if the check digit is shown as a pass/fail light and not as a weighted sum. The model (EAN/UPC module patterns, decoding by ratios, the check digit) is a small algorithm. The layout is a published fact, also documented on Wikipedia, so no data licence is needed. The pitfall is correct. There is one factual flaw in the interaction: an EAN-13 has 13 digits, but only 12 groups of stripes appear. The first digit is hidden in the odd/even pattern of the left six groups. Either use UPC-A (12 digits, 6 + 6, all visible), which is the same symbol as EAN-13 with a leading 0, or say where the 13th digit lives. Reading upside down works because the left and right halves use different patterns, and the page should show that.

fix.interaction: Drag a scanner's red line across a barcode (a UPC-A, the 12-digit form found on many products) and watch what it sees, a trace of dark and light over time, then step through it: a start mark, six groups of stripes, a middle mark, six more and an end mark, each group of two bars and two gaps one digit. Scan slowly, fast or at a slant and the widths all stretch together, so the digits come out the same; scan it upside down and the scanner tells, from the left groups looking different from the right ones, which way to read. Smudge one stripe and the last digit, a check digit, turns the light red: the number is wrong, scan again.
fix.needsSource: none; the UPC-A/EAN-13 symbol layout (95 modules, 7 per digit, L/G/R patterns, check digit) is public structural information (GS1 General Specifications; Wikipedia 'International Article Number', CC BY-SA, for the parity table).

final.title: QR codes
judgeNotes: build 5: A real QR encoder with Reed-Solomon (MIT and Apache libraries exist) and a decoder run on painted damage give an exact failure point; for robustness the decoder should read the cell grid rather than a simulated camera image.

fit-level 4: Painting damage onto a real Reed-Solomon-backed code and watching it still read makes the toy the takeaway; it is distinct from error-correction's Hamming arithmetic and pairs well with barcodes without duplicating them.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from error-correction, which is level 2 and shows Hamming parity checks on bits. This page is the physical object, its finder patterns, and Reed-Solomon tolerance to painted damage, with no arithmetic shown. An honest level 0. It is buildable: qrcode-generator (MIT) encodes, and jsQR (Apache-2.0) decodes a canvas rendered from the SVG. Covering a finder pattern does make decoding fail, as described. The pitfall misses one point: the recoverable fraction (7/15/25/30% for L/M/Q/H) is counted in damaged codewords (bytes), not cells. A count of cells cannot give a fixed failure threshold, because scattered damage touches more codewords than a compact blot. The format information next to the finders is also critical. The pitfall should say this, so the counter is not read as a universal cell budget.

fix.pitfall: The three corner squares hold no message; they are for finding and orienting. The code is not read in a spiral or line by line, and the spare cells are not a copy of the message, so do not say the data is duplicated. The survivable damage (about 7 to 30 percent depending on the level chosen) is counted in damaged bytes, not cells or area: a scatter of specks can break a code that a single blot of the same size does not, so the cell counter is a guide, not a fixed limit.
fix.takeaway: A QR code carries its message plus spare cells computed from it, so a scratched or half-covered code still reads, until too much of the message is spoiled or a corner finder is hidden.

final.title: Wi-Fi around the house
judgeNotes: build 4: A multi-wall indoor loss model (ITU-R P.1238 and per-material losses, freely published) on a grid heatmap, with an SNR-to-rate table and CSMA turn-taking, is a buildable, honest model.
fit-level 4: A router placement map driven by a wall-loss model, with rate adaptation and channel sharing, is practical and visual for beginners, and distinct from wireless-signals.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from wireless-signals, which covers modulation and noise. The level-0 framing (a signal map and a speed gauge, no dB) is honest, and a multi-wall path-loss model with per-material losses plus CSMA-style turn-taking is easy to run in the browser. Two problems. First, the data: 'published indoor loss figures' names no source with a clear licence. ITU-R recommendations are copyrighted, although their formula is a fact. A public-domain source exists: NIST IR 6055, Electromagnetic Signal Attenuation in Construction Materials (Stone, 1997, a US government work), which measured brick, concrete, drywall, glass, plywood and wet wood at 0.5 to 8 GHz. Second, the pitfall's sentence 'Distance does not reduce the router's speed' contradicts the gauge, which does drop with distance. The intended point is that the slowdown is the devices choosing a sturdier, slower way to send, not the signal 'running out'. The page should also not imply that a wall's straight-line shadow is the whole story, since reflections fill in behind walls; a multi-wall model is a simplification and should be named as one.

fix.needs: Attenuation per wall material at 2.4 and 5 GHz: NIST IR 6055, 'Electromagnetic Signal Attenuation in Construction Materials' (W. C. Stone, NIST, 1997; brick, concrete, drywall, glass, plywood, wet wood), for a multi-wall path-loss model; water (fish tank, people) from the same report's wet-material results or textbook absorption values.
fix.needsSource: NIST IR 6055 (US federal government work, public domain; https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/IR/nistir6055.pdf).
fix.pitfall: Wi-Fi is not the internet; a full signal to the router says nothing about the line out of the house. The signal does not stop at an edge: it fades gradually, and the devices then choose a slower, sturdier way of sending so that it can still be read, which is why the gauge drops step by step instead of cutting out. Walls are not perfect shadows either; reflections leak signal around them, which this simple wall-counting model leaves out.

final.title: How Shazam recognises a song
judgeNotes: build 5: STFT, peak picking, pair hashing and an offset histogram over a dozen synthesized clips is the real Wang algorithm at small scale and runs in milliseconds, with no data licensing.
fit-level 4: Constellation hashing with a histogram of time offsets is a superb, distinct mechanism; it honestly needs fourier-transform, a level-2 page, so level 2 is right despite the target mix.
final.verifyNote: No existing page matches audio. compression keeps spectral coefficients for reconstruction, and this page keeps peak pairs for lookup. Level 2 is honest: a spectrogram needs fourier-transform (level 2), and binary (level 1) is also a valid prerequisite. Short-time FFT, peak picking, combinatorial hashing and an offset histogram over a dozen synthesized clips all run in the browser at interactive rates. No data is needed, since the clips are synthesized. The takeaway and pitfall match Wang (2003): the decisive evidence is time-offset alignment, and the method does not find covers or hummed tunes. The batch target asks for few level-2 topics, but that is a selection question, not a flaw.

final.title: Distributed hash tables & consistent hashing
judgeNotes: build 5: Consistent hashing, Chord finger tables and churn with replicas over thousands of simulated nodes are cheap to simulate, and the logarithmic hop count is a measured result.
fit-level 4: Consistent hashing and Chord finger tables show logarithmic hop counts and minimal key movement, a real distributed-systems mechanism distinct from consensus-blockchains.
final.verifyNote: Not on the site: consensus-blockchains is about agreeing on a log, internet about packet routing; nothing shows key placement on a ring, the share of keys that move under consistent hashing compared with modulo, or finger-table routing. Its prerequisite hash-tables-bloom-filters is a level-3 candidate in this pool (computing.json), so the levels are consistent. Level 3 is honest: MIT 6.824 and Brown CS168 teach Chord. The model is a pure algorithm and needs no data. The facts check out: Chord lookups take O(log N) hops (about half of log2 N on average, so about 6 to 12 for thousands of nodes), and adding a node moves only about K/N keys. The pitfall about virtual nodes and about replication versus lookup is correct.

final.title: Elliptic-curve cryptography
judgeNotes: build 5: Chord-and-tangent addition over the reals, a small prime field scatter and double-and-add with BigInt for real curve parameters are an exact, small model; the curve parameters are public standards.

fit-level 4: The chord-and-tangent group law, first over the reals and then over a finite field, is visual and is the real model, a clear level-3 step beyond the modular Diffie-Hellman of cryptography.
final.verifyNote: The page is distinct from cryptography (modular Diffie-Hellman on a clock face) and the level is honest: ECC is taught in university cryptography courses. Curve parameters are public standards. The 256-bit versus about 3,072-bit equivalence is NIST SP 800-57's 128-bit security level. The takeaway is wrong as written, though: adding two points is easy to undo (subtract one), and the one-way step is scalar multiplication. Recovering k from kP is the elliptic-curve discrete log. Small fix.

fix.takeaway: Multiplying a point on a curve by a secret number is quick, but over a finite field nobody knows a practical way to recover the number from the result, so a 256-bit curve key does the job of a 3,000-bit modular one.

final.title: The Kalman filter
judgeNotes: build 5: A 2D constant-velocity Kalman filter with covariance ellipses, sensor fusion and model mismatch is a textbook small linear-algebra model that runs every frame.

fit-level 4: A predict/update cycle with a growing and shrinking covariance ellipse is the real model and a strong, distinct level-3 page; the category is off, though, and it belongs with mathematics or energy (beside feedback-control) rather than networks.
final.verifyNote: Not on the site: feedback-control tunes PID gains and adds sensor noise but never estimates state, and gps solves for position from timing. A 2D constant-velocity Kalman filter with a covariance ellipse runs trivially in the browser and uses synthetic data, so no dataset is needed. Level 3 is honest (MIT OCW 16.322). The prerequisites are at level 2 or below. The pitfall is accurate: the filter is optimal only for linear-Gaussian systems, can be more certain than any one measurement, and a wrong motion model gives confident errors. The 'networks' category is a slight stretch, but the category is information processing, so it is acceptable.

final.title: Radar & sonar
judgeNotes: build 5: Pulse and chirp echoes, a matched filter by FFT correlation, a Doppler range map and noise are a small, honest 1D signal simulation.
fit-level 4: Echo timing, chirps with matched filtering, Doppler and range-Doppler maps are a real signal-processing model, and medical-imaging only mentions ultrasound in passing.
final.verifyNote: Distinct: waves-interference shows a Doppler shift of sound, and medical-imaging reconstructs CT and mentions ultrasound only in passing. Neither shows pulse-echo ranging, chirp pulse compression with a matched filter, or range-Doppler maps. These are 1D signal-processing models that run easily client-side and use synthetic targets, so no data is needed. Level 3 is honest (MIT OCW RES.LL-003 radar course), and the prerequisites are at level 2. The facts check out. Seawater's conductivity absorbs radio waves, so sonar uses sound at about 1,500 m/s, and sound absorption rises steeply with frequency, which is why long-range sonar is low-frequency. Doppler gives only the radial speed. Shaping is the primary way stealth reduces radar cross-section, with absorbent material secondary.

final.title: TCP congestion control
judgeNotes: build 5: A discrete-time bottleneck queue with Reno, CUBIC and delay-based senders produces the real sawtooth, convergence to a fair share and bufferbloat at interactive rates.
fit-level 4: The AIMD sawtooth, convergence to fairness and bufferbloat are a well-known, very drawable control loop that the internet page's resend demo does not cover.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from internet, which only resends lost packets; nothing on the site shows slow start, AIMD, convergence to fairness or bufferbloat. The model is a fluid or packet-level simulation of a bottleneck queue, cheap to run in the browser, with no data. Level 3 is honest (Stanford CS144). The 1986 congestion collapse and Jacobson's 1988 fix support the claim that it keeps the network from collapsing. Small fix: the takeaway says every sender backs off on packet drops, but the page itself compares a delay-based sender, so it should name classic loss-based TCP. The pitfall should also add that AIMD's fair share holds only for flows with equal round-trip times.

fix.takeaway: The Internet has no traffic police: each classic TCP sender probes for its share of the bottleneck by speeding up until the queue overflows and packets drop, then backs off, and that simple rule is what keeps the network from collapsing.
fix.pitfall: Congestion control is not flow control: the receiver's window protects the receiver, and the congestion window protects the network. A loss on a wireless link is often noise rather than congestion, and classic TCP misreads it as a signal to slow down. AIMD's 'fair share' is fair only between flows with similar round-trip times; a flow with a short round-trip time grabs more.

final.title: How a chatbot picks its next word
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A level-0 entry to LLMs with a real counting mechanism a 10-year-old can play; it is distinct from language-models, which shows network probabilities at level 2.

build 5: A bigram or trigram count table over a few public-domain Gutenberg books is tiny, exact and runs instantly; 'read more books' just adds counts, so the model is the honest one and the cards show it directly.
final.verifyNote: It substantially overlaps a sibling level-0 pool entry, autocomplete-spellcheck. That page's second half already shows next-word guesses as counts of which word followed the last one in a pile of books, and its overlapWith ignores this. ngram-text-models covers the same counting idea at level 1. The parts autocomplete does not show are writing by repeated sampling (rolling a die weighted by the counts and feeding the output back in) and the chatbot framing. Narrowing the interaction to those parts keeps it as the level-0 rung of the LLM ladder the user asked for. As written, 'always picking from those counts' is ambiguous; it should be a weighted random pick, not always the top card. Otherwise the level is honest (counts on cards, one button), the data is public domain from Project Gutenberg, and the model runs in the browser. The why URL points to /lessons/8, but the Chatbots and LLMs lesson is reported as the fourth of eight lessons, so cite the unit page instead.

fix.interaction: Play a guessing game against a tiny machine that has read a few children's books: a story stops mid-sentence, you guess the next word, and the machine shows its own guess as a row of word cards, each with a count of how often that word came next in everything it read. Then let it write on its own: each word is drawn by chance like a spinner whose slices are as big as the counts, so it usually picks a common word but sometimes an odd one, and the word it picked becomes the start of the next guess. Press the one button, 'read more books', and watch the cards fill up and its stories get better.
fix.takeaway: A chatbot writes by guessing one word at a time from what usually came next in the text it learned from, adding each guess to the story before making the next, so it picks likely words, not true ones.
fix.overlapWith: autocomplete-spellcheck (proposed, level 0) suggests the single most common next word while you type; this page has the machine write whole stories by drawing words at random in proportion to the counts and feeding each one back in, the loop a chatbot runs. language-models shows the same loop with a real network for a level-2 reader. The next-word half of autocomplete-spellcheck should be cut back so the two pages do not repeat each other.
fix.why: Code.org How AI Works, lesson 'Chatbots and Large Language Models' (grades 6-12): https://code.org/ai/how-ai-works

final.title: How a spam filter decides
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Naive Bayes reduced to word counts that vote is a genuine classifier a 10-year-old can check, and it prepares well for bayes-theorem; the vote weighting must stay as comparisons, not ratios, to remain level 0.
build 5: Naive Bayes word counts on the UCI SMS Spam Collection (CC BY 4.0, confirmed on UCI, about 500 KB) is a small, exact, real classifier whose counts the reader can check.
final.verifyNote: It is distinct from bayes-theorem (a disease-test grid) and from learning-from-data (curve fitting). A word-count classifier is a real model that runs in the browser, and at level 0 it stays honest as counts and votes. There are two problems. (a) The takeaway claims 'A spam filter has no idea what a message means: it counts which words...'. That describes the classic word-count (naive Bayes) filter; modern mail filters also use sender reputation, links and neural networks, so the claim needs to be scoped. (b) The SMS Spam Collection includes adult and crude spam taken from the Grumbletext forum, which is not suitable for readers aged 9 to 13. The page needs a hand-checked, child-safe subset. The licence (CC BY 4.0 on the UCI page) could not be confirmed by search and should be checked on the dataset page before shipping. The 'fr33' trick works as described: an unseen word adds nothing to the vote.

fix.takeaway: This kind of spam filter has no idea what a message means: it counts which words turned up more in past spam than in ordinary messages, which is why spammers misspell and why your 'report spam' clicks teach it.
fix.needs: The SMS Spam Collection (Almeida, Gómez Hidalgo and Silva, UCI Machine Learning Repository, 5,574 messages), reduced to a hand-checked subset of a few hundred messages with adult or crude spam removed, since the audience is children.
fix.needsSource: UCI SMS Spam Collection (https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/228/sms+spam+collection), listed by UCI as CC BY 4.0; confirm the licence line on the dataset page, and ship only a curated child-safe subset.
fix.pitfall: No word is bad: 'free' is only commoner in spam. The filter can be fooled both ways, and how much spam exists overall matters, so a rare kind of message needs stronger evidence; keep that as counts, not Bayes' formula. Do not say this is how every modern mail filter works: real ones also look at the sender, the links and use neural networks.

final.title: Teach a machine to tell things apart
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Nearest-neighbour voting on the reader's own doodles, with a shortcut-learning trap, makes the toy the takeaway; it is an ideal level-0 entry to learning-from-data and distinct from it.
