build 5: k-nearest-neighbours on downsampled drawings is exact and instant in the browser. The reader's drawings need no data, and Quick, Draw! (CC BY 4.0) is optional. The shortcut-by-position trap falls out of the real model.
final.verifyNote: It is distinct from learning-from-data: it is nearest-neighbour classification on downsampled drawings, with no curve fitting. It is buildable in the browser as a real algorithm. The position trap works with a pixel-grid nearest-neighbour vote, so the takeaway can be seen in the graphic. The level-0 level is honest. Quick, Draw! is CC BY 4.0, but its README warns that the moderated drawings may still contain inappropriate content, so a hand-checked subset is needed for children. The pitfall misstates the wolf-and-snow story. In Ribeiro et al. 2016 (LIME) the researchers trained that classifier on purpose on hand-picked photos where every wolf had snow behind it, to test whether people would notice. It was a constructed demonstration, not an accident found in the wild.

fix.needs: Optional: a hand-checked subset of doodles (a few hundred per class) from the Quick, Draw! dataset (Google, CC BY 4.0) as a ready pile of examples; the reader's own drawings need nothing.
fix.needsSource: Quick, Draw! dataset, CC BY 4.0 (https://github.com/googlecreativelab/quickdraw-dataset), optional; its README warns that moderated drawings may still be inappropriate, so ship a hand-checked subset.
fix.pitfall: The machine does not know what a cat is; it compares squares. Do not call the neighbour vote a neural network; neural-networks comes later. If the wolves-in-snow story is told, tell it accurately: researchers (Ribeiro et al., 2016) built that trap on purpose, picking photos where every wolf had snow behind it, to show how a model can learn the background; it was not an accident discovered in a real product.

final.title: Finding groups: k-means
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Promotes a reserve topic with an honest level-1 algorithm a learner can step by hand on penguins, but it duplicates the k-means half of clustering-gaussian-mixtures in this file, so only one of them should keep k-means as its core.

build 5: Lloyd's algorithm, the elbow plot and a DBSCAN contrast on Palmer penguins (CC0) or hand-placed points are tiny exact algorithms. It overlaps heavily with clustering-gaussian-mixtures in the same batch, so one of the two should absorb the other.
final.verifyNote: It is not in the existing catalogue, but it nearly duplicates the pool's clustering-gaussian-mixtures (level 3). That entry's first half is the same step-through of k-means on unlabelled Palmer penguins, plus the same failure on a ring and the same density-based rescue. This level-1 entry also crowds in an elbow plot and a second, density-based algorithm. k-means itself (nearest centre, then average) is honest level-1 material. The fix is to narrow this page to k-means only (assign, move, repeat; k and the starting points; the ring where it fails) and leave the density method and soft Gaussian clustering to the level-3 page. That page should then list this one as a prerequisite and drop its own k-means walkthrough. The title 'Clustering' is too generic. Palmer penguins is CC0, which is confirmed.

fix.title: Finding groups: k-means
fix.interaction: Scatter points by hand or load real penguins measured by bill length and flipper length, with their species hidden, then step k-means: drop k centres, colour every point by its nearest centre, move each centre to the middle of its colour, and repeat until nothing moves. Change k and the starting positions and watch the groups change, reveal the species to compare, and draw two rings, one inside the other, to see k-means cut them in half because it only knows 'nearest centre'.
fix.takeaway: A computer can find groups in data with no labels at all, by alternately assigning points to the nearest centre and moving the centres, but which groups it finds depends on how many it is told to look for and where it starts.
fix.needs: The Palmer penguins measurements (344 penguins, three species).
fix.needsSource: palmerpenguins (Horst, Hill and Gorman), CC0, from Palmer Station LTER (https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/).
fix.pitfall: k-means does not discover the number of groups and finds only compact, roughly round blobs of similar size; different starts give different answers, so run it several times. The groups it finds need not match the species.
fix.overlapWith: clustering-gaussian-mixtures (proposed, level 3) should start where this ends: soft Gaussian clusters with EM and density-based methods, with this page as its prerequisite and no repeat of k-means. Among existing pages, learning-from-data fits labelled points and embeddings shows a map of words that cluster; neither runs an algorithm that finds groups without labels.

final.title: N-gram text models & their limits
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: It has a real counting model and a clear lesson: contexts explode exponentially. It is an honest level-1 bridge between the level-0 next-word game and language-models, though its generation half overlaps that game a little.

build 5: Character n-gram counting and sampling over 1 MB of Tiny Shakespeare (public domain, MIT repo) runs in the browser, and both meters (unseen held-out contexts, longest verbatim copy) are exact computations; a clean, honest model.
final.verifyNote: It is distinct from language-models (a trained network's precomputed probabilities). It is also distinct from the level-0 next-word-guessing-game and autocomplete-spellcheck, because it adds what they lack: the window slider, measured unseen contexts on held-out text, and the drift into verbatim copying. Counting n-grams over about 1 MB of text is quick in the browser. The level-1 level is honest: counts, held-out text and exponential growth fit a high-school reader. The takeaway and pitfall are correct: there are vocabulary-to-the-power-n possible contexts, and smoothing and back-off do not add long-range structure. Shakespeare's text is public domain; the MIT claim for the char-rnn repository was not confirmed by search, but it does not matter if the text is taken straight from Project Gutenberg. Small fixes: say where the text comes from without depending on the repository's licence, and add autocomplete-spellcheck to related.

fix.needs: About 1 MB of Shakespeare's plays (the 'Tiny Shakespeare' extract popularised by Karpathy's char-rnn, or the same plays taken from Project Gutenberg) and the reader's own text.
fix.needsSource: Shakespeare's plays are public domain (Project Gutenberg, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/100); the Tiny Shakespeare file is an extract of them, so its repository's licence does not matter.
fix.overlapWith: language-models shows a trained network's predictions; this page builds the counting model that came before it and measures why counting cannot reach far back. The level-0 pages next-word-guessing-game and autocomplete-spellcheck use one- or two-word counts with no window slider and no held-out measurement.

final.title: Why thinking out loud helps a model
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: It shows on a checkable addition task why fixed compute per token makes written working help, a distinctive and timely mechanism that no page covers.

build 3: Training two tiny addition transformers offline is doable, but the outcome is an empirical result that has to be measured, not asserted. Tiny transformers often learn direct addition fine at trained lengths and fail length generalisation even with a scratchpad unless positions are handled carefully, so the claim about lengths beyond training is at risk.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from every existing page, and buildable as two tiny transformers the project trains itself. But the interaction and takeaway overclaim what the source shows. Nye et al. (arXiv 2112.00114) trained on 1-8 digits and tested on 9-10: the scratchpad model generalised better, but it still degraded, so it does not 'keep going'. Length generalisation is a known weak point for scratchpad models too. 'Fails once the carries outrun its layers' is also wrong as a mechanism. A fixed-depth transformer can represent addition in parallel, and direct addition is learned well when the answer is written least-significant digit first. The gap is clearest when the answer is written most-significant digit first, where the first output digit depends on every carry. Level 3 and the prerequisites are fine.

fix.interaction: Two tiny transformers of the same size were trained by the project on 1- to 8-digit addition with the answer written most-significant digit first: one writes the answer straight away, the other first writes its working (each column's digit sum and carry). Pose sums and step through each model token by token, with the carry chain highlighted: the direct model must settle every carry before its first output digit and errs on long carry chains, while the scratchpad model reads the carry it just wrote back in. An accuracy chart by number of digits and by longest carry chain compares the two, with 9 and 10 digits shown as beyond training, where both fall off but the scratchpad model falls more slowly.
fix.takeaway: A transformer does a fixed amount of computation per token, so writing intermediate steps gives the same model more computation and a place to keep partial results, and it then solves carry-heavy sums the direct model gets wrong.
fix.pitfall: The written steps help because they are computation the model conditions on, not because the model narrates a hidden thought, and in large models the written reasoning is not guaranteed to be a faithful account of how the answer was reached. Do not say transformers cannot add directly (they learn it well when the answer is written least-significant digit first), and do not say a scratchpad solves length generalisation: beyond the trained lengths, both models degrade.

final.title: Serving a language model: the KV cache
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: It explains with a real roofline model why decoding is memory-bound and why batching makes serving cheap; this is distinct from the gpu page's parallel speed-up race and essential to how LLMs are run.

The model is counting arithmetic and bytes over published configurations, so it is client-side and buildable. The takeaway and pitfall are correct. final.title: Position in a transformer: sinusoids & RoPE
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A clean, visual mechanism (order-blind attention, then sinusoids and RoPE rotations) that the transformers page never covers; honest level 3 with the real math.
build 5: Pure math needing no data: permutation equivariance of attention, sinusoidal encodings and RoPE's relative-distance invariance are exact, small computations that render instantly.
final.verifyNote: Partial duplicate. The existing transformers page already has a 'Where a token stands' step. What is new is the geometry of the sinusoidal and rotary schemes and RoPE's dependence on relative distance; the page should narrow to that. 'Push past the training length and compare how each scheme copes' needs trained models for each scheme, which the entry does not provide. fix.pitfall: RoPE does not add a position vector to the embeddings and is not applied to the values. 'Depends only on relative position' holds for the score of one query-key pair, not for the whole network's behaviour beyond the trained length. fix.overlapWith: transformers: that page shows GPT-2's learned position embeddings and states that position must be added; this one shows the sinusoidal and rotary schemes and why rotation makes attention depend on relative distance.

final.title: RLHF: learning from human preferences

final.title: Scaling laws
judgeNotes: fit-level 3: An empirical law, not a causal mechanism, but the Chinchilla compute-optimal split is a real model the graphic can solve; the live retraining is heavy and adds little.

final.title: Speculative decoding
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: The rejection-sampling rule and its histogram that matches the target exactly make an elegant, checkable mechanism, distinct from kv-cache-inference, which it builds on.

build 5: The accept/reject rule with residual resampling is an exact algorithm on two small own models (or even on toy distributions), and the 10,000-sample histogram matching the target is a clean, honest demonstration.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from language-models (sampling) and from the proposed kv-cache-inference (why a decode step is memory-bound). The rejection rule, accept with min(1, p/q) and otherwise resample from the normalized max(0, p-q), is exact and confirmed in the literature, so the takeaway is correct. Level 3 is honest: it is LLM-systems course material, and its prerequisites are L2 and L3. Buildable with a char-level target and a bigram draft over the same vocabulary. Small fixes: the target weights are shipped from the training page rather than trained here; draft and target must share a vocabulary; a fully accepted run of guesses earns one extra token from the target; and the 10,000-sample histogram matches only within sampling noise.

fix.needsSource: None external beyond Tiny Shakespeare (public-domain text; char-rnn repository MIT); the weights are the project's own.
fix.interaction: A cheap draft model guesses the next few tokens and the large target model checks them all in one pass: step through each guess, accepted with probability min(1, p/q) or rejected and replaced by a sample from the leftover distribution max(0, p - q), with p and q drawn as overlapping bar charts. When every guess is accepted, the target's own pass adds one more token for free. Change the number of guesses and swap in a better or worse draft to see the tokens gained per target pass, then run ten thousand samples and watch their histogram converge on the target model's distribution.
fix.pitfall: It is not an approximation: with the rejection rule the output distribution equals the target's (a finite sample histogram matches only up to sampling noise). Accepting only exact matches with the target's top choice is valid only for greedy decoding. The speed-up pays off because a decode pass at small batch is memory-bound, so checking several tokens costs about as much as one; the tiny models on the page are not memory-bound, so the page counts target passes, not seconds.

final.title: Tokenization & byte-pair encoding
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: Building BPE merge by merge and running GPT-2's real merges explains why tokens fall where they do, which goes beyond language-models' display of a given split.

build 5: BPE training on a typed corpus is a small exact algorithm and GPT-2's byte-level tokenizer (regex pre-split plus about 50k merges, a few hundred KB, MIT/modified-MIT) runs instantly in the browser.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from language-models, which only shows text split into tokens; this page builds BPE merge by merge and applies GPT-2's real merges. Level 3 is defensible: university NLP courses teach byte-level BPE, with its regex pre-split and rank-order merging, and the prerequisites are L2. Data: tiktoken is MIT, and OpenAI's gpt-2 repository and the Hugging Face openai-community/gpt2 repository (which ships vocab.json and merges.txt) carry modified-MIT and MIT licences, so it is usable. The takeaway is factually wrong (rule 5): 'never sees letters' is false. GPT-2 has single-character tokens, and rare words and byte fallback do break down to letters. What is true is that the model cannot see the letters inside a merged token. A small rewording fixes it.

fix.takeaway: Tokens are built by greedily merging the most frequent pairs in the training text, so a model sees whole words where text is common and fragments where it is rare, and cannot see the letters inside a token.
fix.pitfall: Merges apply in rank order, not by longest match, so the split is deterministic given the merge list; byte-level BPE never needs an unknown token. Do not say models never see letters (single characters are tokens too), nor that they count letters: inside a merged token the spelling is invisible to them.
fix.needsSource: tiktoken, MIT (confirmed). GPT-2's merge list and vocabulary: OpenAI's gpt-2 repository (modified MIT) and the Hugging Face openai-community/gpt2 repository, tagged MIT, which ships vocab.json and merges.txt (456 kB).

final.title: Training a tiny language model
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A cornerstone level-3 LLM page: real cross-entropy training measured against n-gram baselines, with overfitting visible. Nothing existing trains a language model, and several other candidates build on it.

build 4: A two-layer character transformer with tens of thousands of weights can train live in JS or WebGPU at a few steps per frame, with honest loss curves. The overfitting and data-size sweeps may need precomputed runs to stay interactive; this page is also the infrastructure several other candidates depend on.
final.verifyNote: Distinct and honest at L3: it is the 'Let's build GPT' material, the existing language-models page only reads precomputed probabilities, and the prerequisites are L2 and proposed L1 and L3. Rule 3 risk as written: training to convergence live in the browser for every width, context and data setting is minutes of compute per point, and no browser demo of live transformer training turned up (the TF.js example is an LSTM and warns that browser training is slow). Promising that it beats the 5-gram line is unsafe. A two-layer model with tens of thousands of weights may not beat a well-smoothed char 5-gram within a short browser run, and an unsmoothed 5-gram scores badly on validation, so the line depends on smoothing. Also, 'a fixed order' of sample improvement is an observed tendency, not a law. Fix: train only the default configuration live, in a Web Worker with a fixed seed, ship precomputed curves and samples for the parameter grid, and commit only to the bigram and smoothed trigram lines.

fix.interaction: Press train and a small character-level transformer (two layers, a few tens of thousands of weights) learns Tiny Shakespeare live in the page, with a fixed seed: the training and validation cross-entropy fall on a loss curve with smoothed bigram and trigram models' validation scores drawn as horizontal lines, perplexity is read off beside it, and a sample is written every few hundred steps. Change the model width, the context length and the amount of data to load precomputed runs of the same model (trained offline with the same code) and compare them: bigger models and longer contexts end lower, and with too little data the two curves split as it starts memorising.
fix.takeaway: Training a language model is gradient descent on one number, the average surprise at the next character, and as that number falls the samples go from random letters to plausible spelling to words and line structure.
fix.needs: Tiny Shakespeare; a tiny char-level transformer trained by the page itself for the default configuration (nanoGPT's character-level configuration is the reference), plus the project's own precomputed loss curves and samples for the other settings, trained offline with the same code; smoothed n-gram baselines counted from the same train/validation split.
fix.pitfall: Perplexity is the exponential of the average cross-entropy per token and is comparable only between models with the same tokenizer and the same validation text; a training loss near zero is memorisation, not success. The order in which samples improve is a typical pattern, not a guaranteed sequence.

final.title: Pendulum clocks & the escapement
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A textbook how-it-works mechanism (the weight drives, the pendulum meters) told entirely in counts, and distinct from oscillations-resonance's period plot.

build 5: A pendulum ODE with an anchor that catches the escape wheel and gives a small impulse each swing is a compact, honest simulation, and the period depending on length but not drive weight falls out of it.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from oscillations-resonance, which shows the period of a free pendulum. This page is the catch-and-release escapement and the split between the drive and the timekeeper. The model is buildable: a pendulum ODE with an impulse and lock at each tooth, and a weight-driven escape wheel. Level 0 is honest: the reader counts ticks against a second hand and needs no formulas. It has no prerequisites, and leadsTo oscillations-resonance is level 1. The takeaway and pitfall are sound. Clock-pendulum dynamics (arXiv 1501.03673) shows that more drive raises the amplitude, which shifts the rate only slightly (circular error makes it slower, not faster), so 'hardly changes the rate' and 'a bigger swing does not tick faster' are both correct. No data is needed.

final.title: How a drone steers with four rotors
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A clear mechanism (steering purely by rotor speed differences, yaw from counter-rotating pairs) that fits one-control-at-a-time play and differs from feedback-control, which only holds a drone at a height.

build 5: A small rigid-body ODE (thrust per rotor gives lift, pitch and roll torques; drag torque from spin direction gives yaw) runs trivially in the browser, and each effect the page describes comes straight out of it.
final.verifyNote: The physics is right and the page is distinct from flight (a wing) and feedback-control (PID altitude hold). It is buildable as a rigid body with thrust growing with rotor speed and reaction torque per rotor. Every direction claim checks out: faster back rotors pitch the nose down and the drone moves forward; a faster left pair rolls it right; speeding up the clockwise rotors yaws the body counterclockwise (Parallax multirotor lesson; arXiv 1908.07401). The level-0 rule fails, though. A level-0 page offers one control at a time, and four independent speed dials at once is exactly what it must avoid. The small fix: one control per step (all-up throttle, then a tilt-forward, a tilt-sideways and a turn control), with the four rotor speeds and arrows shown changing as the result. The four-dial sandbox comes only in a final free-play step.

fix.interaction: Each step gives one control, and the drone shows its four rotors with a push arrow and a speed bar on each. Raise the throttle and all four speed up together so the drone rises; push the forward control and watch the back pair speed up, the drone tip and slide forward; push the sideways control and the left pair speeds up so it tips and slides right. Then the turn control speeds up the two rotors that spin clockwise and slows the other two: the lift stays the same but the drone turns on the spot, and if all four spin the same way the body spins helplessly the opposite way. A last step hands over the four rotor speeds directly.

final.title: Diggers and hydraulics: a small push becomes a huge one
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: Pascal's force-for-distance trade, shown with pistons and a digger, is a core primary and KS3 mechanism that no existing page covers and that shows well as a graphic.

build 4: Pascal's principle plus volume conservation is exact and tiny, the air bubble works as a compressible spring, and the boom-arm-bucket is planar linkage kinematics; all of it runs at interactive rates.
final.verifyNote: Distinct (no catalogue page covers fluid pressure or hydraulics) and buildable: area-ratio pistons conserve volume and work, the air bubble compresses by Boyle's law, and the three cylinders drive the arm's linkage kinematics. Level 0 holds if the ratios stay as comparisons (ten times wider area, ten times the push, a tenth of the distance). KS3 schemes of work teach hydraulics as force multiplication. The takeaway is wrong as worded. It says the liquid passes the 'push' on undiminished and then that the wide piston gets many times the push, which contradicts itself and conflates force with pressure, a classic misconception. The liquid passes on the push per bit of area (the pressure), not the total force. Rewrite the takeaway and say this in the pitfall.

fix.takeaway: A trapped liquid passes on the same push on every bit of surface it touches, so a piston with ten times the area gets ten times the push, paid for by moving only a tenth as far.
fix.pitfall: Hydraulics make no energy: the work in equals the work out, and the small piston simply travels much farther. The liquid does not pass on the same total force; it passes on the same push per bit of area, which is why the bigger piston gets more. A liquid barely squashes, which is the whole point; a spongy brake pedal is air in the line.

final.title: Why a light bulb glows (and gets hot)
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A glowing hot wire and where the energy goes, with an LED to compare, is a clear mechanism and energy story that electric-circuits does not show.

build 5: Planck's law at the filament temperature, integrated against the CIE colour-matching and V(lambda) tables (freely downloadable from cvrl.org), gives both the glow colour and the light-versus-heat split honestly and cheaply; the LED comparison needs only a cited luminous efficacy.
final.verifyNote: The page itself is distinct: electric-circuits treats the bulb as a circuit element, and the overlapping pool entry glowing-hot was not selected. Level 0 is honest and the model is buildable: a tungsten filament power balance (resistance rising with temperature, Stefan-Boltzmann radiation) plus Planck's law and the CIE curves, all cheap in the browser. The CIE data checks out: CIE's own open-access datasets carry CC BY-SA 4.0 in their metadata (cie.co.at/data-tables). The problem is a factual error in the LED half. White LED bulbs turn only roughly 30 to 50% of their electricity into light, so the rest is heat. For the same light (about 800 lm, 60 W incandescent against roughly 8 to 9 W LED) the LED's heat falls about tenfold, but it is still larger than its light bar. That heat leaves through the base and heat sink rather than as infrared, so the LED bulb does not 'nearly vanish' or run 'nearly cold'. Saying it does repeats a popular misconception. The fix also states which light bar is shown. An incandescent bulb's visible share is about 2% of its electricity if weighted by eye sensitivity, and roughly 5 to 10% if counted as power in the visible band.

fix.interaction: Slide a dimmer and watch the thin wire inside an old-style bulb go from dark to dull red to orange to white as it heats, while a bar splits what the bulb takes into light you can see and heat. At full brightness the heat bar is dozens of times the light bar, and most of that heat leaves as invisible infrared you feel on your hand. Swap in an LED bulb giving the same light: the electricity it needs, and so its heat bar, shrinks to about a tenth, though the LED still makes more heat than light and warms its base instead of glowing in infrared.
fix.takeaway: An old bulb makes light by heating a wire until it glows white and wastes nearly all its electricity as heat, while an LED makes the same light from about a tenth of the electricity, so far less heat.
fix.pitfall: The wire does not burn: there is no oxygen inside the bulb, which is why a tungsten filament lasts about a thousand hours. Brightness does not rise in step with the dimmer: a little more current makes the wire much hotter, much brighter and whiter. And an LED is not cold: it still turns over half its electricity into heat, only much less electricity overall.
fix.needs: The CIE 1931 colour-matching functions and the photopic V(lambda) curve, to turn the filament's temperature into an on-screen colour and a light-versus-heat split (CIE open-access datasets, CC BY-SA 4.0, cie.co.at/data-tables; also at cvrl.org). Tungsten's resistivity and emissivity against temperature from Jones & Langmuir (1927, General Electric Review), quoted as numbers, or a grey-body emissivity of about 0.4 documented as an approximation. The LED's efficiency is a documented typical value (white LED bulbs at about 90 to 100 lm/W, against about 15 lm/W for incandescent).
fix.needsSource: CIE 1931 CMFs and V(lambda): CIE open-access datasets, CC BY-SA 4.0 (cie.co.at); tungsten property values are published physical constants, cited.

final.title: Toilet flush & siphons
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: The siphon flush and the float valve are a surprising, everyday mechanism no page shows, and they need no formulas.

build 4: A lumped model of tank, bowl and trapway levels, in which the siphon primes once the bend overflows fast enough and breaks when air enters, plus a float valve, runs easily; the priming threshold is a simplification the page should state.
final.verifyNote: Distinct (no existing page shows a siphon; level 0 and a small tank-and-bend flow model are honest and buildable). But the takeaway is stated as true of every toilet, and it is not. Washdown toilets, the usual design in Europe, Japan and Australia, never siphon: the rush from the tank pushes the water over the weir (https://horow.com/blogs/guide/siphon-jet-vs-washdown-toilet-guide-to-choosing-the-right-toilet-flushing-system, https://plumbingconnection.com.au/drainline-transport-waste/). The pitfall explains the siphon as one leg 'outweighing' the other, which is the contested chain model. It also says a slow pour 'drains nothing', when in fact the extra water trickles over the weir and the bowl stays full. Fix: name the siphonic toilet, add a washdown bowl for contrast, and correct the pitfall.

fix.interaction: Press the lever: the flapper lifts, the tank pours into the bowl and the bowl's water climbs toward the top of the bend behind it. The moment it spills over fast enough, the whole bend fills and the bowl drains itself, fast, until air gets in and it gurgles to a stop. Then pour a bucket in slowly or quickly to find what starts the siphon, swap in a wide-bend washdown bowl that never siphons and only pushes the extra water over the top, and watch the float rise with the refilling tank and shut its own valve.
fix.takeaway: In a siphonic toilet the tank only has to fill the bend behind the bowl; once it is full, the water running down the long side drains the bowl by itself until air gets in and breaks the siphon.
fix.pitfall: The flush is not suction, and not every toilet siphons. In a siphonic toilet, gravity pulls the water down the long side of the bend while the air pressing on the bowl pushes more water in behind it. A slow pour never fills the bend and just trickles over the top, so the bowl stays full. Washdown toilets, the usual kind in much of Europe, never siphon: the tank's rush pushes the water over the weir.

final.title: ABS & the tire's grip
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A tyre slip curve with wheel dynamics and a cycling controller is a real nonlinear model a vehicle-engineering student meets, it has a crisp counter-intuitive takeaway, and it is distinct from feedback-control's PID.

build 5: A quarter-car wheel ODE with a magic-formula or Burckhardt slip curve and a bang-bang slip controller is a classic small real-time model. The curve coefficients are widely reproduced numeric values, so no licensing problem.
final.verifyNote: Distinct from feedback-control (a nonlinear slip-curve plant with a bang-bang cycler). Level 3 is honest: wheel-slip dynamics belong to university vehicle-dynamics courses, and a quarter-car wheel ODE runs easily in the browser. The data source is the problem. 'Pacejka coefficients, published values, textbook paywalled' names no usable dataset. The Burckhardt friction-slip model is the standard open alternative, and its coefficient sets for dry asphalt, wet asphalt and snow are reproduced in openly readable papers such as arXiv 2211.10336 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10336). Coefficients are facts, so they can be reused. I found no peer-reviewed ice set, so ice must use a cited low-mu curve or be dropped. The interaction also says the peak is at 10 to 20 percent slip on every surface, but on snow the curve peaks at much lower slip.

fix.interaction: Brake a car from highway speed on dry asphalt, wet asphalt or snow: each wheel's spin follows its own equation of motion, and the tire's braking force follows a measured friction-against-slip curve whose peak sits near ten to twenty percent slip on dry asphalt and at smaller slip on snow, falling away as the wheel locks; the stopping distance is marked on the road. Brake too hard with ABS off and the wheel locks, the car slides further and no longer answers the steering; switch ABS on and watch the controller cycle the brake pressure to keep each wheel near the peak.
fix.needs: Tire friction-slip curves from the Burckhardt model, mu = c1(1 - e^(-c2 s)) - c3 s, with its published coefficient sets for dry asphalt, wet asphalt and snow (reproduced openly, e.g. arXiv:2211.10336); an icy surface only if a cited coefficient set is found.
fix.needsSource: Burckhardt friction-slip coefficients, published in the open literature (arXiv:2211.10336 among others); coefficients are facts, freely reusable.

final.title: Why a bicycle balances itself
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A classic level-3 result (the linearised Whipple model's eigenvalues, self-stability without gyroscopes) with a surprising takeaway, an everyday object and nothing like it on the site, though it fits physics better than energy.

build 5: The Whipple benchmark is a 4-state linear system whose eigenvalues against speed and time responses compute instantly. The parameters are openly tabulated, and the self-stable band and the countersteer are visible in the graphic.
final.verifyNote: The takeaway and pitfall are factually wrong for the model the page would run. I computed the eigenvalues of the Meijaard et al. 2007 benchmark bicycle. With all terms in place it is self-stable from about 4.3 to 6.0 m/s, the published band. With the wheels' spin angular momentum removed (S_R = S_F = 0 in C1 and K2), it is not self-stable at any speed from 0 to 15 m/s. So the page would show the opposite of its takeaway. What is true (Kooijman et al., Science 2011, https://swov.nl/en/publicatie/bicycle-can-be-self-stable-without-gyroscopic-or-caster-effects) is that neither the gyroscopic effect nor trail is necessary in principle: a specially designed 'two-mass-skate' bicycle balances with neither. On an ordinary bicycle, both contribute. The rest holds up: distinct from feedback-control, level 3 is honest (linearised multibody eigenvalues), the model is a 4x4 linear system that runs at interactive rates, and the parameters are published.

fix.interaction: Push a riderless bicycle at a chosen speed and let its linearized equations of motion run: below a certain speed it slowly falls, in a middle band it wobbles and recovers on its own, and above it it slowly leans away. Drag the speed and watch the eigenvalues of lean and steer cross the stability boundary; change the trail, the head angle and the front-wheel mass, cancel the gyroscopic effect of the wheels and the trail in turn and see the ordinary bicycle lose its self-stable band, then load the two-mass-skate design that balances with neither; finally steer left and watch the bike first lean right.
fix.takeaway: A riderless bicycle balances itself in a band of speeds because a lean makes its front wheel steer into the fall, and that self-steering comes from the geometry and mass of the whole front assembly, not from any single effect such as the wheels' gyroscopic spin.
fix.pitfall: Neither 'the gyroscope keeps it up' nor 'the gyroscope plays no part' is right. On the standard benchmark bicycle, cancelling the wheels' gyroscopic effect removes its self-stable speed band. Yet Kooijman et al. (2011) built a bicycle that balances with neither a gyroscopic effect nor trail. Self-stability comes from several effects working together.
fix.needs: The benchmark bicycle parameters and linearized equations of Meijaard, Papadopoulos, Ruina and Schwab (2007, Proc. R. Soc. A, doi:10.1098/rspa.2007.1857), reproduced openly at http://ruina.tam.cornell.edu/research/topics/bicycle_mechanics/, and the two-mass-skate parameters of Kooijman et al. (2011, Science 332:339, doi:10.1126/science.1201959).
fix.needsSource: Meijaard et al. 2007 benchmark and Kooijman et al. 2011 parameters (published numerical values, which are facts; the benchmark is openly reproduced on the Cornell page).

final.title: Combined-cycle power plants
judgeNotes: fit-level 4: A real Brayton model on a T-s diagram with the compressor's share of the work and a bottoming steam cycle is core level-3 thermodynamics and distinct from heat-engines' Otto loop; it also underpins jet-engines.

build 5: A Brayton cycle with component efficiencies and public-domain NASA cp polynomials, plus a bottoming steam cycle, gives a live T-s diagram and an efficiency well above 60 percent from a small, honest calculation.
final.verifyNote: The Brayton half substantially duplicates jet-engines, a level-3 page in this same pool that already plots a gas turbine on a T-s diagram from its cycle, station by station. The steam half duplicates steam-power-cycles, which already has real steam properties and a T-s diagram. The only new mechanism is the coupling: the heat-recovery boiler and its pinch point, and why the pair beats either engine alone. The pitfall is also muddled. It mixes up net work and efficiency: ideal Brayton efficiency rises without limit with pressure ratio, and with component losses both work and efficiency peak, at different ratios. 'Over half the turbine work' is only true on average: typical back-work ratios are 40 to 80 percent (Purdue ME 200 notes, https://engineering.purdue.edu/~wassgren/teaching/ME20000/NotesAndReading/Lec39_Reading_Wassgren.pdf). Fix: narrow the page to the combined cycle, built on jet-engines and steam-power-cycles. The data (NASA Glenn polynomials, public domain; IAPWS-IF97, free) is fine.

fix.title: Combined-cycle power plants
fix.interaction: Set a gas turbine's pressure ratio and turbine inlet temperature and watch its exhaust leave at several hundred degrees; then route that exhaust through a heat-recovery steam generator drawn as a temperature-heat diagram, the cooling gas line above the heating water-and-steam line. Drag the steam pressure and the pinch-point gap, add a second and third pressure level, and see the two lines hug more closely, the stack temperature fall and the plant's combined efficiency climb past 60 percent.
fix.takeaway: A combined-cycle plant reaches about 60 percent efficiency because a steam cycle turns the gas turbine's hot exhaust into extra work, and it recovers more the more closely the steam's heating line can follow the cooling exhaust.
fix.pitfall: The best gas turbine for a combined cycle is not the most efficient stand-alone one. A lower pressure ratio leaves a hotter exhaust for the steam cycle, so the plant's optimum pressure ratio is below the gas turbine's own. And the steam cycle burns no extra fuel: it only uses heat that would otherwise go up the stack.
fix.overlapWith: jet-engines and steam-power-cycles each show one of the two cycles on a T-s diagram; this page shows only what neither does: the heat-recovery boiler's temperature-heat matching and pinch point that couple them into one plant.
fix.needs: Specific heats of air and combustion products as functions of temperature (NASA Glenn thermodynamic polynomial coefficients, US government, public domain); water and steam properties from IAPWS-IF97 (freely published), as in steam-power-cycles.

final.title: Heat pumps & refrigeration
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: A Reserve item with high everyday demand, and a vapour-compression cycle on a real-refrigerant p-h diagram is exactly what the field teaches; heat-engines never runs a cycle backward or shows a phase change.

build 5: A vapor-compression cycle on a p-h diagram from refrigerant properties tabulated offline from MIT-licensed CoolProp is an honest, instant model. CO2 needs supercritical tables but that is just more table.
final.verifyNote: Sound. No existing page runs a cycle backward or uses a real refrigerant with a phase change. Level 3 is honest: Thermodynamics I covers the vapor-compression cycle on a p-h diagram (Purdue ME 200). CoolProp is MIT-licensed and covers R-134a, propane (R-290) and CO2 (R-744), transcritical CO2 included, and property tables or fits can be shipped to the browser. The takeaway and pitfall are correct: the Carnot COP falls as the temperature lift grows. Two small improvements. This pool also proposes refrigerator (L0) and heat-pumps (L1), so the three form a ladder; the L1 page should be a prerequisite, and overlapWith should say how the L3 page differs from it. The Reserve item 'Heat pumps' is now claimed by the L1 page.

fix.overlapWith: heat-pumps (L1, this batch) runs the loop with bars for heat delivered against work; this page adds what it leaves out: a real refrigerant on a p-h diagram, compressor losses, subcooling and superheat, the Carnot comparison and the transcritical CO2 cycle. heat-engines never runs a cycle backward and has no phase change.

final.title: Wind turbines & the Betz limit
judgeNotes: fit-level 5: It is a high-demand subject with a crisp mechanism (actuator-disc momentum balance to the Betz limit, then blade-element-momentum with real NREL polars), honestly level 3, and it extends flight to the whole rotor without duplicating it.

build 5: Actuator-disc momentum theory is analytic, and a blade-element-momentum iteration over about 20 elements with the NREL S809 polar (openly published by a US-government lab) converges in milliseconds, so both stages are small, honest, interactive models.
final.verifyNote: Distinct: flight shows a single airfoil section and lift, while no existing energy page has momentum theory, the Betz limit or a rotor. The level-3 claim is honest, because actuator disc plus blade-element-momentum is the core of university wind-energy courses (Penn State AERSP 583). Its prerequisite flight is level 2, which is allowed. BEM with a polar lookup runs easily at interactive rates. The takeaway (16/27 is about 59%, reached at a = 1/3) and the pitfall are correct. One weak point is the licence claim: NREL is a contractor-operated lab, so its outputs are not automatically public domain. The NREL 5-MW airfoil tables ship in the OpenFAST r-test repository, which is labelled Apache-2.0, and that is the source to cite. The interaction should also name tip-loss and the high-induction (Glauert) correction, so the BEM model stays honest at high tip-speed ratios.

fix.needs: Lift and drag polars of wind-turbine airfoils: the NREL 5-MW reference turbine's AeroData tables (DU and NACA64 sections) as distributed in the OpenFAST r-test repository (github.com/OpenFAST/r-test, Apache-2.0), with blade chord and twist from the same reference turbine; NACA airfoil data (public domain) as a fallback.
fix.needsSource: OpenFAST r-test repository, 5MW_Baseline/AeroData (Apache-2.0; check the repository LICENSE when shipping); NACA reports (public domain).
fix.interaction: Start with an actuator disc: drag how much the air slows through the rotor and watch the stream tube widen, the thrust and power change, and the power coefficient peak at 16/27 when the air leaving is slowed to a third. Then replace the disc with real blades: set the tip-speed ratio and the blade pitch, and a blade-element-momentum model (with tip-loss and the high-induction correction) using measured airfoil polars computes the angle of attack along the blade, the power coefficient against tip-speed ratio, and the power curve against wind speed with pitch control holding power at rated above rated wind.

gapEntries.title: Camouflage: you are the hungry bird
gapEntries.interaction: Moths of many shades rest on a tree trunk and the reader is the bird: tap every moth you spot before the timer runs out. The survivors lay eggs that look like their parents, give or take a little, and the next generation appears; after a few rounds the reader flips the bark from pale to sooty and keeps hunting.
gapEntries.takeaway: The moths you fail to see are the ones that have babies, so after a few generations the moths match the bark, and when the bark changes, so do the moths.
gapEntries.needs: Bark textures, either procedurally generated or public-domain or CC0 photographs from Wikimedia Commons; the moth population model needs no data.
gapEntries.pitfall: A moth does not change colour to hide, and no moth chooses its colour; the population changes because the visible ones are eaten before they breed.
gapEntries.why: England national curriculum, KS2 Year 6 'Evolution and inheritance': identify how animals and plants are adapted to suit their environment and that adaptation may lead to evolution (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study); NGSS MS-LS4-4 (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ls4-4-biological-evolution-unity-and-diversity).
gapEntries.overlapWith: evolution: that page runs a population with sliders for mutation, population size and environment; here the reader is the predator, and the selection is their own clicking, which is the level-0 doorway into that page.
gapEntries.needsSource: none, or CC0/public-domain bark photographs (Wikimedia Commons)
gapEntries.verifyNote: Sound in substance. The model (heritable shade with small variation, plus the reader's own predation) is real and cheap. The takeaway shows in the graphic, and the pitfall is right. The page differs from evolution, where the predator is a slider, because here the reader is the predator. leadsTo evolution and meiosis-inheritance are both existing level-1 pages. The weak point is the 'why': a CliffsNotes page is not a curriculum source. The KS2 Year 6 statutory requirement on adaptation and the NGSS standard should be cited directly.
judgeNotes: build 4: The heritable-shade population model with the reader as selective predator is a real, simple genetic model rather than a picture to tap, since the next generation is computed from the survivors; procedural bark avoids licence questions.
fit-level 5: The reader acting as the selective predator makes the mechanism the toy itself, a strong level-0 doorway to evolution that is distinct from that page's slider-driven population.

gapEntries.title: Induction heads: how a model copies from its prompt
gapEntries.interaction: Scrub through the training of a tiny two-layer, attention-only transformer (one head per layer) on sequences that repeat partway through, from a fixed-seed run whose checkpoints ship with the page, or retrain it live; watch the loss sit on a plateau and then fall suddenly. At any checkpoint, hover a token in a test sequence to see each head's attention: after the drop, the layer-1 head looks at the previous token and the layer-2 head attends to whatever followed the earlier copy of the current token. Switch off either head and the in-context copying stops.
gapEntries.takeaway: A transformer learns to continue a pattern seen earlier in its prompt with a two-head circuit, one head marking each token's predecessor and another finding the earlier match and copying what followed, and that circuit appears all at once as a sudden drop in the loss.
gapEntries.needs: Checkpoints of a tiny attention-only transformer trained on synthetic repeated-token sequences, produced by the project (or trained live in the browser), following the setup of Olsson et al. 2022 and Singh et al. 2024 (arXiv 2404.07129); no external data.
gapEntries.pitfall: Induction heads do not explain all in-context learning: they copy what is already in the context, and abilities such as learning a new mapping from examples need more than this circuit.
gapEntries.why: Anthropic's 'In-context Learning and Induction Heads' and its follow-ups are a core mechanistic-interpretability result, studied at ICML 2024: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07129
gapEntries.overlapWith: transformers: that page shows the attention weights of a trained model on fixed sentences; this one trains a model live, shows one specific two-head circuit forming during a phase change, and tests it by switching heads off.
gapEntries.needsSource: none (synthetic data, model trained by the project; only the published method is reused)
gapEntries.verifyNote: Not a duplicate: transformers shows the attention of a fixed pretrained model, while this page trains a model, shows the circuit forming and switches heads off. The level and prerequisites are honest (transformers is level 3; training-a-tiny-language-model is a proposed level-3 slug), and the takeaway and pitfall agree with Olsson et al. 2022 and Singh et al. 2024. Two weaknesses. First, the needsSource asserts that arXiv 2404.07129 is CC BY 4.0, which I could not verify; it is also irrelevant, because only the method is used and the data are synthetic. Second, no source gives a training time for a CPU or browser run, and the plateau before the phase change can be long. The page should use one head per layer, so that switching a head off is clean, and keep a fixed-seed run with precomputed checkpoints as the scrubbable default, with live training as an option.
judgeNotes: build 4: A two-layer, one-head-per-layer attention-only transformer on synthetic repeated sequences is small enough to ship checkpoints or train live in a browser, and head ablation is cheap; reproducing the loss plateau and drop reliably takes care with seeds and hyperparameters, so shipped checkpoints should be the default.

fit-level 5: A real, trainable two-layer circuit with a phase change and ablations is exactly the detailed LLM mechanism the AI tilt asks for, honest at level 3 and distinct from the static attention view on transformers.
gapEntries.kept: runner-up (outranks no topic it could replace)

gapEntries.title: Sequence alignment: lining up genes across species
gapEntries.interaction: Pick two real protein sequences, such as human and mouse haemoglobin or human and yeast cytochrome c, and fill the dynamic-programming grid cell by cell: each cell takes the best of a match, a gap in one sequence or a gap in the other, and the traceback lights up the optimal alignment. Change the gap penalty or swap BLOSUM62 for an identity matrix and the best alignment shifts; switch from global (Needleman-Wunsch) to local (Smith-Waterman) and only the conserved core survives. Shuffle one sequence a hundred times and the page plots the shuffled scores against the real one.
gapEntries.takeaway: The best alignment of two sequences is found exactly by building it from the best alignments of their prefixes, and a real relative scores far above what shuffled sequences reach.
gapEntries.needs: A handful of protein sequences from UniProt (CC BY 4.0), and the BLOSUM62 substitution matrix (Henikoff & Henikoff 1992, PNAS 89:10915). The matrix is a table of numerical values, freely redistributed in the NCBI BLAST distribution and in Biopython (BSD licence). Cite the paper.
gapEntries.pitfall: An alignment is not proof of shared ancestry: any two sequences have an optimal alignment, and it changes with the scoring matrix and gap penalties; only a score far above the shuffled-sequence background is evidence of homology.
gapEntries.why: MIT 6.047 Computational Biology notes open with global and local alignment by dynamic programming (Needleman-Wunsch, Smith-Waterman): https://ocw.mit.edu/ans7870/6/6.047/f15/MIT6_047F15_Compiled.pdf
gapEntries.overlapWith: dna-to-protein translates one gene; this page compares two genes, and its model is the dynamic-programming alignment and its score statistics, which no existing or proposed page covers (dna-fingerprinting matches repeat lengths, not sequences).
gapEntries.needsSource: UniProt sequences (CC BY 4.0); BLOSUM62, a published numerical table freely redistributed with NCBI BLAST and Biopython (BSD); openly usable with citation
gapEntries.verifyNote: Sound topic, level and prerequisites (dna-to-protein and evolution are both level 1), and Needleman-Wunsch/Smith-Waterman on two short proteins plus 100 shuffles runs easily in the browser. It does not duplicate dna-to-protein or the proposed dna-fingerprinting. The licence claim is wrong, though: BLOSUM62 is not a U.S. government work. Henikoff & Henikoff published it in PNAS in 1992 from the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center and HHMI, not from a federal agency. It is a table of numerical facts, freely redistributed with NCBI BLAST and Biopython (BSD), so it is usable, but Needs must not call it public domain as a government work.
judgeNotes: build 5: Needleman-Wunsch/Smith-Waterman on two ~150-residue sequences is a small O(nm) DP that fills and traces back instantly, the shuffle test is 100 more runs, and UniProt (CC BY 4.0) plus the BLOSUM62 table are openly usable.

fit-level 4: A real dynamic-programming mechanism (Needleman-Wunsch/Smith-Waterman with BLOSUM62 and a shuffled-score background) that bioinformatics students learn, distinct from dna-to-protein and dna-fingerprinting, at an honest level 3.
gapEntries.kept: runner-up (outranks no topic it could replace)

gapEntries.title: Queues: why a nearly busy server is so slow
gapEntries.interaction: Packets (or customers) arrive at random at a router with one output link; set the arrival rate and the service rate and watch the queue grow and drain while a live plot tracks the average wait against the load. Push the utilisation from 50% to 90% to 99% and the wait curve climbs toward a wall, matching Little's law and the M/M/1 formula drawn over the simulated points; make the arrivals or the packet sizes more regular and the same load queues much less.
gapEntries.takeaway: Waiting time stays small until a server is nearly fully busy and then grows without bound, and randomness in the arrivals makes the queue long even when capacity exceeds demand on average.
gapEntries.pitfall: A link that is busy 90% of the time is not 'with 10% to spare': the mean delay at 90% load is about five times that at 50%, and at 99% it is fifty times; average capacity above average demand does not mean no queue.
gapEntries.why: MIT 6.263J Data Communication Networks devotes its core sessions to Little's theorem and the M/M/1 queue: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/electrical-engineering-and-computer-science/6-263j-data-communication-networks-fall-2002/calendar
gapEntries.overlapWith: tcp-congestion-control (proposed) shows senders reacting to a full bottleneck buffer; this page is the queue itself: random arrivals, Little's law and the delay-versus-load curve, with no feedback from the sender.
gapEntries.verifyNote: internet and the proposed tcp-congestion-control do not show the delay-versus-load curve or Little's law. A discrete-event M/M/1 simulation (and M/D/1 for regular service) runs easily client-side. The pitfall's numbers are correct: the M/M/1 sojourn time is proportional to 1/(1-rho), giving 2, 10 and 100 at 50%, 90% and 99% load, so ratios of 5x and 50x. Regular arrivals or service lowering the queue is Pollaczek-Khinchine. The MIT 6.263J signal is apt, prerequisites are existing, and no data is needed.
judgeNotes: build 5: A discrete-event M/M/1 (and M/D/1) simulation with the analytic curve overlaid is tiny, exact and needs no data; the wall near 100% load is visible straight from the plot.

fit-level 4: The delay-versus-load wall, M/M/1 and Little's law form a counterintuitive mechanism a simulation shows well, honest at level 3 and distinct from internet and the proposed tcp-congestion-control.
gapEntries.kept: runner-up (outranks no topic it could replace)

gapEntries.title: Switching power supplies: how a charger changes voltage
gapEntries.interaction: Flip a transistor on and off thousands of times a second in a buck converter and watch the inductor current ramp up and down while the capacitor smooths the output; drag the duty cycle and the output settles at that fraction of the input voltage. Compare against a linear regulator dropping the same voltage across a resistor and see the heat meters diverge; lower the switching frequency or shrink the inductor and the ripple grows until the current hits zero, then rearrange the same parts into a boost converter that steps voltage up.
gapEntries.takeaway: A switching converter changes voltage by chopping it and averaging it with an inductor and a capacitor, so it stores and releases energy rather than burning the excess as heat, and output current can exceed input current.
gapEntries.pitfall: A buck converter is not a resistor that drops voltage: ideally it loses no energy, so stepping 20 V down to 5 V draws about a quarter of the output current from the source.
gapEntries.why: MIT 6.334 Power Electronics covers the modelling, analysis and control of DC-DC converters, inverters and rectifiers: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-334-power-electronics-spring-2007/pages/syllabus/
gapEntries.overlapWith: power-grid uses transformers to change AC voltage; this page is the DC-DC switching converter (in every phone charger, laptop and solar inverter), modelled as a piecewise-linear circuit ODE, which no page shows.
gapEntries.verifyNote: No catalogue page shows DC-DC conversion: power-grid uses transformers on AC. A buck or boost converter is a piecewise-linear ODE that is trivial to integrate client-side. The physics checks out: Vout = D*Vin, and the ripple grows until discontinuous conduction as the frequency or inductance falls. The pitfall checks out too: ideally 20 V to 5 V draws about a quarter of the output current. Level 3 fits a topic from an MIT 6.334 syllabus, prerequisites are existing level-1 and level-2 slugs, and no data is needed.
judgeNotes: build 5: An ideal-switch buck/boost converter is a piecewise-linear two-state ODE (inductor current and capacitor voltage) that integrates exactly and fast; ripple, discontinuous conduction and the efficiency comparison all come out of the model.

fit-level 4: An everyday device (every charger) with a clear piecewise-linear circuit mechanism and the surprising result that output current exceeds input current, distinct from power-grid; university power-electronics material, so level 3 is honest.
gapEntries.kept: runner-up (outranks no topic it could replace)

gapEntries.title: Why the Moon doesn't fall down
gapEntries.interaction: A cannon stands on a very tall mountain on a round Earth. The reader picks a single thing, how hard to fire, and launches balls one after another; slow ones land close, faster ones land farther around the curve, and one fast enough falls all the way around and comes back to the mountain. A last step swaps the ball for the Moon, far away and moving sideways.
gapEntries.takeaway: Everything thrown falls, but a ball moving sideways fast enough keeps missing the curving ground, so it goes round forever: that is what the Moon and the space station are doing.
gapEntries.needs: none (Newtonian gravity integrated for one body around Earth; Earth radius and surface gravity are standard constants)
gapEntries.pitfall: There is gravity in space: astronauts float because they are falling together with their station, not because gravity has switched off. The Moon is not held up by anything.
gapEntries.why: Newton's cannonball is the standard answer to the child's question why the Moon doesn't fall (https://eg.bucknell.edu/physics/astronomy/astr101/specials/newtscannon.html); KS2 Year 5 requires that unsupported objects fall towards Earth because of gravity, and NGSS 5-PS2-1 that gravity pulls objects down.
gapEntries.overlapWith: orbits-kepler: that page launches bodies around a star to derive ellipses and Kepler's laws with overlays and two planets; this one has one control, starts from throwing a ball, and only reaches the idea that an orbit is falling and missing.
gapEntries.verifyNote: Sound as a level-0 on-ramp. It shares its core idea with orbits-kepler, whose takeaway is that an orbit is continuous free fall. But orbits-kepler is level 1, with speed and direction controls, area overlays, period plots and two planets. This page has one control, starts from throwing a ball, and lists orbits-kepler in leadsTo, which is exactly the level-0 pattern the plan asks for. Its prerequisite earth-is-a-ball is a proposed level-0 space topic, so the level is fine. One-body Newtonian integration is trivial in a browser, and no data is needed. The pitfalls (there is gravity in space, astronauts are in free fall) are correct, and the Newton's cannon grounding is standard (Bucknell ASTR101 page). Minor build note: the circular-speed ball returns to the mountain from behind, so the mountain should be thin or the ball drawn passing just over it.
judgeNotes: build 5: Newton's cannon is a single-body inverse-square integration with real Earth constants, trivially interactive, and the falling-and-missing takeaway is visible in the trajectories.

fit-level 4: Newton's cannon is the classic one-control level-0 doorway to orbits-kepler; that page already states that an orbit is free fall, but without formulas and with one control this page is a fair beginner entry rather than a duplicate.
gapEntries.kept: runner-up (outranks no topic it could replace)

gapEntries.title: Friction: why things slide or stick
gapEntries.interaction: A block sits on a ramp. The reader raises the ramp slowly, one control, and sees the exact angle at which the block starts to slide; then changes the surface (ice, wood, carpet, rubber) or the block's weight and tries again, while an arrow shows the grip of the surface growing to match the pull down the slope until it can't.
gapEntries.takeaway: Friction grips just as hard as it needs to, up to a limit set by the two surfaces, so a heavier block slips at the same angle but ice lets go much sooner than rubber.
gapEntries.needs: Typical static friction coefficients for a few surface pairs from one edition of OpenStax College Physics 2e, Table 5.1 (CC BY 4.0); cite the edition, since rows such as steel on ice differ between versions.
gapEntries.pitfall: Heavier things do not slip later on the same ramp, and for hard surfaces such as wood, metal or ice the size of the touching area hardly matters (soft rubber is the exception); friction is also not only a nuisance, since walking and braking need it.
gapEntries.why: KS2 Year 5 statutory: identify the effects of air resistance, water resistance and friction that act between moving surfaces (https://its.teachit.co.uk/resources/primary/forces-ks2); NGSS 3-PS2-1 balanced and unbalanced forces.
gapEntries.overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page has forces changing motion with carts and projectiles; this one isolates the grip between two surfaces on a tilting ramp, the starting point for kids before any equation.
gapEntries.needsSource: OpenStax College Physics friction table, CC BY 4.0
gapEntries.verifyNote: The page is sound overall. It is a genuine level-0 toy with one control (the ramp angle), the KS2 Year 5 and NGSS 3-PS2-1 signal fits, and it differs from newtons-laws, which has no friction-on-ramp page. The takeaway is right, since the slip angle tan(theta) = mu_s does not depend on weight. OpenStax College Physics (Table 5.1) is CC BY 4.0. One part needs a fix: the pitfall states flatly that friction never depends on contact area, yet the page includes rubber, where area and deformation do matter (tyres). Hedge it to the rule of thumb for hard surfaces. Also note that OpenStax editions differ on some rows (steel on ice static 0.4 vs 0.04), so the page should cite one edition and use rows consistently.
judgeNotes: build 5: A static-friction threshold on an inclined plane (tan theta = mu_s) with force arrows is a small honest model; OpenStax friction coefficients are CC BY 4.0, provided the edition is cited.
fit-level 4: A tilting ramp with a slip angle is a concrete, formula-free mechanism that newtons-laws does not isolate, and it suits a 10-year-old.
gapEntries.kept: runner-up (outranks no topic it could replace)

gapEntries.title: Learning by treats: how a robot learns by trying
gapEntries.interaction: A little robot pup sits in a small room with a small biscuit close by, a big bone farther away and a puddle in between. Press play: at first it wanders at random; when it reaches a treat, the tile it stepped from glows warmer, and run after run the warmth spreads back across the floor until the pup walks a glowing path straight to it. One control: how often it tries something new instead of following the warmest tiles. Turn it to zero and the pup keeps settling for the near biscuit; give it some curiosity and it finds the bone.
gapEntries.takeaway: Nobody tells the robot the way; it gets better only because the steps that led to a treat are remembered and tried again, and it needs some random tries to find a better route.
gapEntries.needs: none (tabular Q-learning on a small grid, run live in the browser)
gapEntries.pitfall: The robot does not understand or want the biscuit, and it is not given the map; it only adjusts numbers on tiles. The rewards it is given, not good intentions, decide what it learns, so a badly placed reward teaches the wrong thing.
gapEntries.why: AI4K12 big idea 3, learning, sets grade-band progressions for grades 3-5 and 6-8 (https://www.raspberrypi.org/blog/ai-education-ai4k12-big-ideas-ai-thinking/); reward-trained models (game players, chatbot tuning) are the AI kids already hear about.
gapEntries.overlapWith: reinforcement-learning: that level-2 page exposes value tables, discount factor and learning rate on a paintable grid; this one has one control and a pup-and-treat story, as the level-0 entry to the AI track (and later to rlhf-alignment).
gapEntries.verifyNote: Sound as the level-0 doorway to reinforcement-learning (leadsTo learning-from-data is the only level-1 AI page, so acceptable), and all related slugs exist in the batch. But the interaction misdescribes the model it names: tabular one-step Q-learning does not warm 'the floor tiles that led there' after a single success; only the tile next to the biscuit gains value, and the warmth spreads backward one tile per run. Saying otherwise would be untrue, and the honest version is itself a good thing to watch. The exploration control also has no visible payoff unless the room holds a worse treat that greedy following settles on, so the room needs a near small treat and a far bigger one.
judgeNotes: build 5: Tabular Q-learning with epsilon-greedy exploration on a small grid runs live in milliseconds, and the local-optimum-versus-exploration takeaway falls out of the real algorithm.

fit-level 4: A one-control, pup-and-treat version of value learning gives the AI track a level-0 entry, in line with the AI-heavy tilt; it overlaps reinforcement-learning in mechanism but is pitched honestly as a beginner doorway.
gapEntries.kept: runner-up (outranks no topic it could replace)

gapEntries.title: Superposition: more features than neurons
gapEntries.interaction: Train a tiny network in the browser to squeeze five input features through two hidden neurons and rebuild them, and see each feature's direction drawn as an arrow in the 2D hidden space. Slide how rarely each feature is active: with dense features the network keeps two of them at right angles and drops the rest; sparser, it packs four as two pairs of opposite arrows; sparser still, the arrows spread into a pentagon that stores all five, at the cost of some interference. Change the importance of each feature and watch which ones lose their arrows.
gapEntries.takeaway: When features are rarely active at the same time, a network stores more of them than it has dimensions by sharing directions among them and accepting some interference, and the arrangement jumps between distinct shapes (two at right angles, opposite pairs, a pentagon) as sparsity grows.
gapEntries.needs: None: the toy model (ReLU output, tied weights, importance-weighted loss) trains in the browser in seconds, as in Elhage et al. 2022, 'Toy Models of Superposition' (Transformer Circuits).
gapEntries.pitfall: The page must not claim that each neuron in a real LLM stands for one concept, nor that this toy proves exactly how large models store facts; superposition is why single neurons are often hard to interpret.
gapEntries.why: 3Blue1Brown's 'How might LLMs store facts' (Deep Learning chapter 7) ends on the superposition hypothesis: https://3blue1brown.substack.com/p/how-might-llms-store-facts-chapter
gapEntries.overlapWith: embeddings: that page shows the directions of pretrained word vectors; this one trains a network live to show how and when it packs more features than dimensions into one space.
gapEntries.needsSource: none (trained in the browser on synthetic data)
gapEntries.verifyNote: The model is the right one: Elhage et al.'s 5-to-2 ReLU toy trains in seconds in the browser. Not a duplicate, and the level and prerequisites are honest. But the takeaway misstates the geometry. In the five-feature pentagon the arrows sit 72 degrees apart, not 'nearly opposite'; opposite (antipodal) pairs belong to an intermediate stage. As sparsity rises, the toy goes from two features at right angles, to two antipodal pairs (four features), to a pentagon of five. The change therefore comes in distinct jumps, not as one switch from 'drop the extras' to 'pack them all in'. The interaction also skips that middle stage.
judgeNotes: build 5: The Elhage et al. 5-to-2 ReLU tied-weight toy model trains in seconds in plain JS, and the antipodal-pair and pentagon geometries are reproducible results that show directly as arrows.
fit-level 4: The toy model of superposition trains live in the browser and shows geometric phase changes, a key interpretability idea that embeddings does not cover, and it is honest at level 3.
gapEntries.kept: runner-up (outranks no topic it could replace)

gapEntries.title: Drug receptors: dose-response, agonists & antagonists
gapEntries.interaction: Add a drug to a dish of cells and watch it bind receptors by mass action while a log dose-response curve builds point by point; set the drug's affinity and efficacy separately and see potency move the curve sideways while efficacy sets its height. Add a competitive antagonist and the curve slides right in parallel by the Schild ratio, add a non-competitive one and the maximum drops; remove most receptors and a full agonist still gives a full response until its spare receptors run out, while a partial agonist starts blocking the full one.
gapEntries.takeaway: How strongly a drug binds and how strongly it activates are separate properties: a competitive blocker slides the dose-response curve sideways, while a non-competitive one lowers its ceiling once the tissue's spare receptors are used up.
gapEntries.needs: Optional: affinities of a few real agonists and antagonists (e.g. at the beta-adrenergic or mu-opioid receptor) from the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology (database under the Open Database License, ODbL; text content CC BY-SA 4.0). The model itself (operational model, Gaddum-Schild) needs no data.
gapEntries.pitfall: Potency is not efficacy: a more potent drug is not a stronger one, and a maximal response does not mean every receptor is occupied, since many tissues have spare receptors.
gapEntries.why: MIT OCW HST.151 Principles of Pharmacology, lecture 1 'Drug-Receptor Interactions' (mass action, full and partial agonists, reversible and irreversible antagonists): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/hst-151-principles-of-pharmacology-spring-2005/pages/lecture-notes/
gapEntries.overlapWith: pharmacokinetics-dosing (proposed) follows how the body moves a drug's concentration over time; this page is pharmacodynamics, what that concentration does at the receptor, with agonism, antagonism and spare receptors.
gapEntries.needsSource: none required; optional IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology data, ODbL (database) / CC BY-SA 4.0 (text)
gapEntries.verifyNote: The model (mass action, the operational model, Gaddum-Schild) is sound and distinct from pharmacokinetics-dosing, but three things need small changes. (1) The takeaway says a non-competitive blocker lowers the ceiling, which contradicts the page's own spare-receptor feature. With a receptor reserve, an irreversible or non-competitive antagonist first shifts the curve right and lowers the maximum only once the reserve is used up (Furchgott analysis). (2) The why signal is a Wikipedia article, not a curriculum or demand signal; MIT OCW HST.151 Principles of Pharmacology, lecture 1 'Drug-Receptor Interactions', covers it. (3) The IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology database is licensed ODbL; only its text content is CC BY-SA 4.0.
judgeNotes: build 4: The operational model and Gaddum-Schild equations are closed-form, with mass-action binding animated on top; it is honest but mostly evaluates curves rather than simulating, and the optional IUPHAR data is ODbL/CC BY-SA, so share-alike must be honoured if used.

fit-level 4: Mass-action binding, Schild shifts and spare receptors are the real pharmacodynamics model a pharmacology student learns, and the page pairs cleanly with the proposed pharmacokinetics page without overlapping it.
gapEntries.kept: runner-up (outranks no topic it could replace)

gapEntries.title: Retrieval: how a chatbot looks things up
gapEntries.interaction: Pick one of several questions about a small shelf of documents. Watch the documents split into chunks and embed as points; the question becomes a point too, and the nearest chunks light up and are pasted into the prompt. Change the chunk size and the number of chunks retrieved, or remove the document that holds the answer, and compare a small model's next-token probabilities for the answer with and without the retrieved text (precomputed for every combination).
gapEntries.takeaway: A chatbot that 'searches' does not change its weights: it finds the passages whose embeddings sit closest to the question and puts them into the prompt, so its answer is only as good as what retrieval put there.
gapEntries.needs: A small document set, either public-domain texts (for example NASA or US government pages) or Simple English Wikipedia excerpts (CC BY-SA 4.0); embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0), run in the browser or precomputed; next-token probabilities with and without context from a small open model such as SmolLM2-135M-Instruct (Apache 2.0), precomputed.
gapEntries.pitfall: Retrieval does not make answers true: a model can still ignore or misread the retrieved passage, and the nearest chunk by embedding is not always the one that answers the question.
gapEntries.why: Stanford CS224V lists retrieval-augmented generation among its topics (https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224v), and Stanford CS25 recorded a lecture on retrieval-augmented language models (https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs25/recordings).
gapEntries.overlapWith: embeddings: that page measures nearness between word vectors; this one uses nearness between question and passage vectors to choose what goes into a language model's prompt, and shows the effect on its answer.
gapEntries.needsSource: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0); SmolLM2 (Apache 2.0); documents public domain or CC BY-SA 4.0 (share-alike must be honoured)
gapEntries.verifyNote: Not a duplicate of embeddings or language-models, and the licences hold up: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and SmolLM2 are Apache 2.0, and Simple English Wikipedia is CC BY-SA 4.0, whose share-alike requirement is noted. Three problems. (1) The interaction says 'Ask a question', which implies free text, but the next-token probabilities are precomputed, so only a fixed set of questions works across the combinations of chunk size, number of chunks and removed document. (2) The 'why' signal is a dev.to blog post, which is weak; Stanford courses teach retrieval-augmented generation (CS224V lists it; CS25 has Douwe Kiela's lecture on retrieval-augmented language models). (3) The page needs nothing from the level-3 transformers page; embeddings and language-models (both level 2) are enough.
judgeNotes: build 4: Chunking and nearest-neighbour retrieval with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0) are real and cheap, but the generation side is a precomputed SmolLM2 (Apache 2.0) table over every combination of question, chunk size, k and removed document, so the control grid must stay small; it is honest if labelled as precomputed real model outputs, with CC BY-SA honoured for any Wikipedia text.

fit-level 4: Retrieval into the prompt is central to how deployed chatbots work and fills a gap in the LLM set, with a real mechanism (embedding nearness, then a change in next-token probabilities); the mechanism is simple enough that level 2 or 3 both fit, and level 3 is acceptable given its prerequisites.
gapEntries.kept: runner-up (outranks no topic it could replace)

gapEntries.title: Microwave ovens & their hot spots
gapEntries.interaction: Switch on a microwave oven seen from above: a wave simulation fills the metal box, and a slab of food warms where the field is strong, shown as a heat map. Stop the turntable to see fixed hot and cold spots, start it to even them out, and lay a chocolate bar across the floor to measure the gap between melted spots against the wavelength.
gapEntries.takeaway: Microwaves reflecting off the metal walls form a standing pattern of strong and weak spots that stays fixed in the box, which is why food heats unevenly and why the turntable moves the food through it.
gapEntries.needs: None: a 2D finite-difference wave (or Helmholtz) solver in a rectangular cavity at 2.45 GHz with a lossy dielectric slab; standard permittivity values for water and food from textbook tables.
gapEntries.pitfall: 2.45 GHz is not a special resonance of water molecules, and microwaves do not cook food from the inside out; they heat the outer few centimetres, and the chocolate spacing is only roughly half a free-space wavelength because the cavity's modes are not a simple standing wave.
gapEntries.why: The chocolate-in-the-microwave speed-of-light experiment is a classic school lesson: https://www.bu.edu/gk12/loren/lesson_microwave.html
gapEntries.overlapWith: waves-interference: that page shows standing waves and interference on strings and in open space; this one applies them in a closed metal box with an absorbing load, where the pattern decides what gets hot.
gapEntries.verifyNote: Sound. The prerequisite waves-interference is level 1, the same as the candidate. It does not duplicate waves-interference or wireless-signals: neither shows a closed metal cavity with an absorbing load, a heat map or a turntable. The model is a 2D Helmholtz or FDTD solve on a grid of about 30 by 30 cm at a 12 cm wavelength. That is small enough to compute once, and heating accumulated over the turntable angle can be drawn as a pure function of time. The physics in the pitfall checks out: 2.45 GHz is not a water resonance (water's broad absorption peaks near 20 GHz and above), penetration depth is about 1 to 3 cm, and the chocolate experiment is a standard school lesson (the BU GK-12 URL resolves). Permittivities for water and food are textbook values, so no licence problem. Caveat for the builder: a top-down 2D field is a simplification of a 3D oven's modes, and the page should not claim a quantitatively real oven pattern.
judgeNotes: build 4: A 2D FDTD or Helmholtz solve in a rectangular cavity at 2.45 GHz with a lossy slab is feasible on a modest grid, and rotating the load to time-average the heating is cheap; the real oven is a 3D problem, so the 2D cut must be stated, but the hot-spot spacing comes out honestly.
fit-level 4: An everyday device whose standing-wave hot spots and chocolate-bar measurement apply waves-interference to a closed cavity, making it a distinct and honest level-1 page.
gapEntries.kept: runner-up (outranks no topic it could replace)

gapEntries.title: Static electricity: why a balloon sticks to the wall
